Description: Welcome to the Cartography of Memory. It begins here. I was born in St. Paul, Minnesota, on September 11th, 1989. This place is not a memory. It serves as an origin, the start of a route. From here in every direction, you'll find chronotopes from my life––moments and places fused together in memory and narrative. In this exhibit, you can follow them chronologically, thematically, spatially. Each map rendering serves as a different version of this experimental memoir. Zoom out, move around, or read chronologically to learn more.

I grew up in Afton, Minnesota, at town that gets its name from a poem––"Sweet Afton" by Robert Burns. It's a small town of roughly 2,000 people on the outskirts of the Twin Cities. Afton: quiet, wooded, green, a river town with meandering hills down to the St. Croix Valley. It's one of the oldest places in Minnesota, full of ancient hillsides and ravines. The forests, no longer old growth, but nonetheless lush and thick. Much of my childhood I spent in those woods. I lived long summer days in dirty clothes, playing outside. And as I grew older, I took long bike rides down to the river to swim. Then in the dark winters I was holed up at home, reading. So much of my life was lived here that no one memory encapsulates this place. There's just a remembrance of that recurring feeling of childhood, an Afton stillness where I hear the frogs and bugs chirping in the trees on summer nights, or where I feel the hollow wind on cold winter mornings, or the crunch of snow under my feet. These remembrances cut to the marrow. They remove all else in the way of my thinking, and I can imagine like a child again.

Duluth was a recurring backdrop of my childhood and remains one of my favorite cities. My mother grew up here. We used to spend weekends visiting my grandmother. She was a kooky lady. She had one of those grandma houses––old, cluttered, stuffy. I was always worried about getting pinpricks from sewing needles left out on the furniture. The basement was dark, dank, full of the shadows of things in storage. My grandmother insisted on spraying herself with perfume whenever we arrived. She'd walk up the stairs after greeting us then return smelling like orange blossoms and white tea. The best part of visiting was the creek. We'd play in it all day long. It curved around the back yard, past the clothes line and the gravel parking. Then we'd come in for dinner, or we'd head out to one of the few restaurants my grandmother approved of in town. The family corralled into the car and drove down the steep drop of the city into Lake Superior. The views of the wide waters of that sacred lake stay engrained in my mind. It's a cold, old city with handsome houses and a forested background. But then there's the lake, the imposing feature. I think it was a good place for my mother to grow up. But then I think that lake and its coldness made her want to run away sometimes.

Location: Selma's Ice Cream Parlor, Afton, MN
Description: Selma's Ice Cream Parlor is a landmark in Afton. Every summer, I would make pilgrimages to Selma's on my bike, peddling down the windy roads into the valley, for ice cream. Selma's has been in business since 1913. Its first proprietor, Selma Swanson, opened shop with her husband. When he passed away, she ran the business herself until 1966. In a town with little else save the post office, a marina, and a couple restaurants, Selma's was a Godsend for a child who needed something to do. But before I was old enough to go on my own, my family took me and my sisters sometimes in the summer. The old wood floors creaked as we took our place in the line that always wrapped around the room, and we'd shuffle with it until the ice cream counter appeared before us, and I'd pick out my cone and flavors. As I grew older, I came to love chocolate cherry Bordeaux on a waffle cone. I'd toss my bike onto the grass out front and meet with friends and we'd get our ice cream and pass the time, as children do.

During family trips up north, we would often swing West a ways to visit my godparents in Grand Rapids. I don't remember much about the town of Grand Rapids. I only have a rich compilation of memories of Lake Pokegama and my godparents' home. They lived atop a steep hill that descended to the lake. The hillside was covered by forest, a dense forest. Across the lake was their family retreat. We would pontoon across the waters and spend long summer days in the hammock, playing foosball, lazing about. This place was my own personal Pine Island. It made me grow to adore that deeply Minnesotan landscape of birch, pine, loon, and lake water. That far north, the sun stays up past 9pm in the height of summer. I would read outside in peace as a child and enjoy the quiet wilderness.

Location: St. Francis of Assisi Church, Lakeland, MN
Description: This was the Catholic church where my family attended. We were not devout Catholics, but I think my mother would occasionally catch some of that infamous Catholic guilt and try to tamper it with Sunday visits. I also think she wanted the childcare that came with the church community. So I was baptized here, and we went to services and attended church school some evenings. I remember the frankincense and robes and decorum. The dull hymns. I remember the classrooms of fellow children fidgeting through Bible stories. I eventually received the Sacrament of Confirmation, but I didn't return to church afterward, except to attend my mother's funeral, which was held here.

This is a steak restaurant in a log cabin tucked away on a county road. It claims some local lore as a bootlegging spot owned by Al Capone during the Prohibition. Who knows if any of it is true, but it's part of the experience, an experience I associated with fine dining as a child, because this was the fanciest restaurant my family would visit. It was always cramped and busy. The servers told the local lore to each table. One time, they showed us the cellar door behind the bar where the booze was purportedly hidden. Another time, my sister got locked in the bathroom. She screamed so loud the whole restaurant stopped what it was doing. A crowd of folks stood by while my father futzed with the door, finally getting it open and letting out my traumatized sister who just didn't understand how to work the latch.

Location: Joshua Taylor Building, Lake Elmo, MN
Description: This was the location of my dad's office, a place where I spent many a school day afternoon waiting for him to finish work. These afternoons were not as boring as you might expect. They had sodas and chips. Down the old lumber ramp––a long, descending walkway tiled over––I'd go to the back room where there was a Compaq Presario with Age of Empires on it. I got to play as long as no one else needed the computer. For most of my childhood, there was no desktop at home, so that bulky machine in my dad's office was a delight. But then, I grew older. Eventually I was set to task here, mowing the lawn and shoveling the snow at the building. The lawn was small but tedious. It wrapped around the parking lot and had a wood fence I had to maneuver around. The shoveling could take forever. The sidewalks were wide and the walkways around the parking lot were long, and when the snow was heavy, I'd have a hard time finishing before we had to head home.

Pickwick  was my grandmother's favorite restaurant. It's been here, overlooking Lake Superior, for over a century. As a kid, it felt like the epitome of an old person's restaurant. Wood paneling, frescos, stained glass windows. A menu with smoked fish, sausage, and cheese. We used to go here, if there was something to celebrate. Back then, I felt like it was too crusty, but my opinion has since changed. It's a remarkable place with a menu and interior that takes you back in time. It feels like eating where ancient fishermen ate. It feels like a captured part of the city's history, like a place that has yet to know time.

Canal Park lies between the expanse of Lake Superior and the steep hillsides of Duluth. Whenever we visited my grandmother, we would go to the park for an afternoon. It gave us kids something to do. The lake walk always felt like miles and miles of walking. There were seagulls that would descend upon you, if you carried food. The air was always crisp with the cold of the lake. Towering over the park is the Aerial Lift Bridge which rises and falls for incoming cargo ships––big, exciting things when you're a child. I loved those walks along the park. They were always the same but remained exciting each time.

Good old Borderline Video. It's where, on slow Friday nights, my family would go to pick out a VHS or two. We never had Netflix. We didn't have cable. We lived too far away from any national chains like Blockbuster. We only had Borderline Video. It was the authentic experience––a small, privately owned VHS rental shop with a total film junkie behind the counter. It made movie nights different, more intentional. I used to love going in there and seeing the big cardboard cutouts promoting blockbusters. I loved debating with my sisters about which movies to rent. My mother was the one who always took us. My father didn't care for movies unless they were westerns from his childhood. But my mother liked to get us excited to watch something. It was part of a strategy, I'm sure––let the kids pick out movies so they'll be preoccupied for an evening––and it always worked. Of course, Borderline Video is no longer in business, but every time I pass the old location, I am overwhelmed with nostalgia. There was something special about having to travel to a place to pick out your entertainment.

Golden Crown has been a staple in the Stillwater community for my entire life. It remains one of the few Chinese restaurants in the  St. Croix River Valley. I can vividly remember the booths and tables, the carpeted floor. The smell––fried food, soy sauce, peanuts, and garlic––when we stepped in to grab our takeout. It's that quintessential Americanized version of Chinese, the kind I still shamelessly adore. I love getting the fortune cookies or reading the Chinese zodiac. The family that ran the place always had their teenagers working, running food and taking orders. I don't know if it's still a family business, but I hope so. I hope nothing about it has changed.

The Science Museum of Minnesota, a repository of memories––those dinosaur exhibits and the tornado machine and the musical stairs. The big taxidermy bears, the IMAX theater. I ended up here more than once for birthday parties and school field trips. I don't have any memories of going with my family, just memories in large groups of excited kids. I liked the fossils. I liked thinking about gargantuan animals roaming the earth. The wonder of those exhibits felt like wandering the woods back home. But it was more communal. This museum provided new dimensions to my interest in the natural world––social and historical dimensions. It also instilled an appreciation for community spaces of knowledge, and made me a museum visitor for life.

When I was very young, my aunt and uncle lived in the suburbs of Chicago. We only visited them once, to my recollection. On that trip, we went to the Field Museum and strolled the white halls with colossal dinosaurs, elephants–beasts of every kind. It was just once, but it left an impression. I've been a dedicated museum visitor ever since. Alongside trips to the Science Museum of Minnesota, it was one my my most formative museum experiences.

Grand Marais is an unspoiled place in my memory. It's a small harbor town on Lake Superior, an artists' retreat and tourist destination. It is surrounded by lake and bluffs, the edenic palette of green and blue in the summers, a tundra of white by fall. The small shops on streets along the shore are full of independent vendors, antiques, handmade wares. It is a place of homely pleasures. We used to go as a family and walk the streets, enter the general stores, seek out agates on the rocky shores. You would think it was a dull time for a child, but no––the whole peacefulness of Grand Marais against the brutal, expansive lake was something that even a child must admire. I sometimes dream of retreating here today. I could move my bookshop into a little building and stay for as long as life would let me.

Afton Alps is a ski area tucked into the bluffs near the St. Croix River. It was just fifteen minutes from my childhood home. The longest runs were no longer than a few football fields, but it was a good place to learn to ski. It used to be dirt cheap, too, until Vail Resorts bought it. My earliest memories here feature my father who taught me to ski. With great patience, he took my sisters and I up the chairlifts and down the bunny hill, over and over again. Soon we were traversing the slopes like a pack of speedy bombers, my father pacing around us, corralling us down. By the time I was fifteen, I was good enough to become a ski instructor. But I only ever taught a few lessons. I chose instead to ski all day and skip the required check-ins, and so the job was essentially a free season pass. Of course, they didn't hire me back the next year. But then, fast forward to 2013, I returned again as a chairlift operator (to get another season pass). That job was dreadful. I would watch the chairs go round and round while standing in the bitter Minnesota cold. I only took one shift a week. The rest of the time, I would enjoy the hills and drink with friends in the chalets.

Location: Sven and Ole's Pizza, Grand Marais, MN
Description: Sven and Ole's Pizza has been a staple in Grand Marais for decades. It's pretty good––my childhood self would give it five stars. They serve pizza with oversized toppings, big giant bites of sausage and pepperoni buried in mounds of cheese. The interior has some seriously kitschy, "Up North" vibes. Picture taxidermy deer, rusty saws on the walls, a pair of antique skis. These decorations overlay what would otherwise be a typical pizza parlor. And then there are the cartoon mascots––Sven and Ole themselves––on the signs and laminated menus. I'm sure some local Scandinavian drew them decades ago. One wears a yellow raincoat, the other a plaid shirt and trousers. I remember us kids insisting on a stop for pizza every time Sven and Ole came into view.

Location: Ben Franklin Department Store, Grand Marais, MN
Description: During trips to Grand Marais, my siblings and I would insist on visiting the Ben Franklin Department Store. This business relied on the many families passing dull days in cabins up there. It was stocked with little entertainments. We always went to peruse their offerings of Fuzzy Posters. If you're not familiar, a Fuzzy Poster is a coloring canvas with a white image laid into velvet. They usually come with markers for coloring in the white space against the black velvet. We would choose from the many psychedelic patterns––mushrooms, unicorns, filigree, kaleidoscopic shapes. Then on slow afternoons we'd color our Fuzzy Posters and relax. They were good fun, an odd tradition, but the best part was picking them out at the Ben Franklin Department Store.

This was the second elementary school I attended. I'd catch the bus with my younger sister and shuffle into the building on sleepy mornings as a child. My teachers––Mr. Kostynick, Ms. Klancher––got us settled each day. I'd gab and play with friends in the hallways lined with lockers, and I'd eat those generic lunches of milk and pizza. And I'd dream longingly of recess. My favorite game was wall ball. Or lava tag. Or tetherball. Or swinging on the swing set. I remember auditorium events. I remember reading in the school library. I have a whole constellation of memories, most of them small and pleasant. It was a good school. I may not remember much in terms of what I learned here. But I remember friends and fun. In those early grades, I built positive associations with education. I think that's most important. Those associations were broken at times, in junior high and high school, but they stuck with me enough to find a resurgence when I got to college.

Schmigg's was a burger joint and bar for several years in my childhood. We would stop in occasionally, when they had dollar burger nights. The family that owned it lived in the apartment upstairs. Outside, in a fenced-in area, they kept llamas. I have no idea why, but it was always a highlight to go see the llamas on burger night. One time––I remember it clearly––we went to feed the llamas and one spit cud at my mother. She was horrified. My sisters and I could not believe it, either. I never trusted a llama again in my life. They are dubious creatures. But eventually, Schmigg's closed and the place became vacant, and the llamas went away. Then, years later, a new bar opened in the space. At that point I was in my early twenties. It was called Shiner's and it became a regular hangout spot when some of my closest friends took jobs there. It had the same tables and booths, the same energy. I'd go for bar food and company and sometimes on weekends we'd have the place to ourselves after closing time. We'd play pool, chat, sit in the empty bar. Life felt a little too easy and aimless those days. Then at some point around 2016, Shiner's closed, but by then I'd left Minnesota. This bar and the apartment upstairs are still around, but I don't think they've been occupied since.

The Belwin Conservancy is a nonprofit that owns thousands of acres of land near my childhood home. It was always sort of a mystery––I didn't understand Belwin's purpose because it was never accurately explained to me. My father, a man who adamantly opposes neighbors in general, but especially those with resources and power, would rail against Belwin Conservancy for buying up all the land in the valley and closing it off from hunters. He always framed their conservation efforts as foolish, ridiculous. Yet the result of Belwin's work was a largely free and natural landscape for me to explore as a child. I could not overlook it. I adored that place, I loved wandering the woods and creeks and revitalized prairies. As I got older, I learned more about its mission and in strides I removed the fog of my family's biases. It is one such example of my personal growth away from inherited beliefs and ideologies, one that came early. To this day, when I think of "place," I think of natural landscape first and foremost––an association rooted in my childhood adventures in Belwin Conservancy. Without being told, I somehow could sense it was closer to the true natural state of the place where I grew up. A revitalized landscape, an example of good conservation work.

The Phipp's Center in downtown Hudson was a place where an array of events were hosted. I used to loathe my sister's dance recitals here, but now I remember them fondly. I also remember going to a stage adaptation of The Hobbit, perhaps my first ever experience with live theater. The space also had an art gallery where I would slink away during my sister's dance lessons. For a time, they exhibited some of my mother's textile art and weavings. I am proud of her for that. It was the only time I remember her artwork appearing outside our family home. In the narrow corridor to the side of the dance studio, the textiles hung and spotlights shined down on them, creating a kind of sleepy backlit space that was more interesting, at least, than dance lessons.

Lowell Park in downtown Stillwater stretches across the edge of the St. Croix River. In the Spring, it serves as a floodplain. In the mid-to-late summer, it's a place for leisure and festivities. With a perfect view of the Stillwater Lift Bridge––the landmark that defines the town––this park hosts the 4th of July fireworks and picnics and other events. We used to go here often as a family, but my finest memories of downtown Stillwater and Lowell Park come from my teenage years. It was the place to be seen in the summer. In late July, it was the spot of a big festival called Lumberjack Days. This had all the refinements of a small town carnival, but with a local theme. There were woodcutting competitions, log rolling, and other lumber-related entertainments. Burly Paul Bunyan mascots walked amongst the crowds. My teenage friends and I would gather during the festival and get into mischief. It was a safe place to be kids.

Because I grew up in such a secluded place, there were no restaurants that delivered, except Jimmy's Pizza. As a kid, it was the pinnacle of cuisine, the ultimate experience. To get pizza delivered felt like an indulgence reserved for kings and queens. I remember the logo––a pizza with one slice lifted off the pan. At its cut edge, the cheese hung down, spelling "Jimmy's". It was pretty good. Better than you would expect, at least. But to my dismay, it closed sometime in the 2010s. I suppose I could have seen it coming. The restaurant was hardly noticeable. It was off County Road 18 on a gravel lot. It was in a double-wide with a small awning at the front. Inside, it was just four or five tables and a kitchen. The area it serviced had a population of maybe 6,000 people. Yet it was the only option, a monopoly on food delivery. If only more folks had appreciated Jimmy's Pizza as much as I did as a kid.

At the heart of Afton sits Steamboat Park, a little grove in the valley where I used to meet with childhood friends. I'd bike down the winding county roads to get here. I'd stop Selma's across the street, to get my ice cream. The park has a basketball court, a playground, a gazebo, tables, trees. It's a fine little park that rests on sacred ground. Every 4th of July, it fills with people from all over the county to attend the annual parade. Those parades were a highlight of my earliest summers. They were quintessentially American parades. The floats and cars and folks on horseback tossed candy into the crowds. Red, white, and blue streamers ran from the light posts. There was usually a folk band playing patriotic tunes under the gazebo. Fireworks popped from unseen places off the adjacent streets. From the park grills, you could smell the charcoal smoke and meats carried with the breeze. My family brought picnic blankets. We'd watch the parade go by and take it all in.

Once, in 1999, my mother decided to go to the Winnipeg Folk Festival. My father was not interested, so my mother corralled my younger sister and I and drove us to the Canadian Border. I had never been to a music festival before. It was picnicky, fun. That year it rained torrentially and the festival grounds were mud. I remember tromping around in it, and my mother shrugging it off. I don't know why it didn't become a tradition. It remains my idea of Canada––a woodsy, folksy, picnic nation where the weather doesn't bother anyone.

Crocker Park just had a spare baseball field a few blocks from the bridge to Wisconsin. I used to have baseball practice here. I'd bike to practice, stopping at Tom Thumb along the way, to get some Mike & Ikes and gatorade. I played through junior high, but once I was about fifteen, my athletic career ended, replaced instead by teenage debauchery and hourly jobs. But I always missed Crocker Park and those days taking fielders from first base or swinging for the fences. It wasn't much of a baseball diamond, but it's where I learned to play. Sometimes my dad would stop by after work and help coach. Then we'd load up my bike in the back of his truck and drive home, tired and happy.

The St. Croix River is the defining geographic feature of my life. I associate myself with this river, this place, more than anywhere else. It runs from its headwaters in northern Wisconsin to its confluence with the Mississippi River at Prescott and Hastings. It serves as the border of the county where I grew up. In Afton, my hometown, it widens, forming Lake St. Croix. Further north, past Stillwater, it narrows, creating inlets and sandbars. Still further upstream it carves itself through steep crags and dense foliage. Along its banks, you'll find the cleanest water out of fresh streams. The church where I was baptized overlooked the river. All the hills and creeks of my childhood ran toward it. I used to swim into Lake St. Croix to cool off after long days biking across town. I used to meet my friends at the beach. I used to work for the riverboat company in Stillwater, spending endless summer days on the river. I used to kayak from O'Brien State Park to downtown, stopping to rest on the sandy banks. Despite its long geographic track and perpetual movement, the St. Croix River remains a single static feature of my most formative years. It is a sacred river, a spirit embodied by the place, a spirit I came to know well through lots of moments in its presence.

Valley Creek cuts through Afton and meets the St. Croix River on a wooded floodplain. This creek is skinny and shrouded by maples, oaks, and willows. It runs way up the hillside, to Lake Edith. At various sections, I used to wade in its cold waters, explore its oxbows and pools, dig into its rocks and mud. Yet my best memories of Valley Creek occurred at its confluence with the river. When the water was high, you could paddle a canoe or kayak way up into the creek––paddle between trees and stumps and blankets of leaves buoyed up by the water. Up the stream, vast communities of turtles gathered and sat on logs and other natural debris. The fish splashed in the mud, seeking out bugs and critters to eat, and scarce beams of light made it through the canopy and twinkled off their scales. It was a lively place at high water. It was pleasant to paddle in the shade.

Today at this spot stands US Bank Stadium, a polygonal structure of glass and steel. It is an acquired taste, but not so much as its predecessor: the Metrodome. It's the Metrodome that I remember fondly. It was a big white bubble on the horizon of the city where I used to go for Twins' games with my dad. It was always cold inside. The blue stadium seats were clunky, stiff. The white canvas ceiling camouflaged baseballs as they soared into the air. I loved it––the Dome Dogs, the silly mascot races in between innings, the crowd doing The Wave. I'm sure US Bank Stadium is a great experience, too, but the Metrodome still exists here in my memory.

If you were to pass Cully Park, you'd probably think nothing of it. It's got a baseball diamond, a basketball court, and a gravel parking lot. Yet this little park became the locus of a whole social network of kids after school––from about fifth grade until high school graduation. I'm not sure why we chose this place as a designated meetup spot. Perhaps it was mere inertia formed by our school bus routes early in life. In any case, though, you could go to Cully Park any day of the week and wait awhile. Eventually, friends arrived with no prompting or explanation. When we were tweens, we'd play on the basketball court. By high school, we transitioned to standing in the parking lot and talking and getting into trouble. The surrounding neighborhood was full of kids my age. I lived up in the woods so my journeys to Cully Park were longer than most, but I went often. I always envied my friends with close neighbors who could wander around their streets and find company. That was not something I experienced unless I biked a long ways or hopped off the school bus early to get to places like Cully Park.

Tom Thumb was a gas station like any other. I believe today it's a Super America. Yet it will always be a special place, the place where I'd stop with friends for all manner of occasion. It was a pitstop for sodas and candy before baseball practice, before heading to friends' houses, before meeting up in the park. Behind the building is a wooden fence with a missing panel where we used to crawl through and follow a trail, the shortcut to Tom Thumb. It was the only place within walking distance where candy and drinks could be purchased. Lots of kids would go here after school each day. It was one nexus of the neighborhood that brought us together.

Location: St. Croix Public Beach, Lakeland, MN
Description: Down by the river, beyond the shaded little houses in this neighborhood, is a public beach none too crowded. It stretches maybe 100 yards along the water, with clean, beige sand and a wide view across Lake St. Croix. I used to stop by on my bike on hot summer days and dive into the water to cool off. The beach is sort of hidden behind the levee and the dense neighborhood surrounding it. From the county road, you would never know it was there, unless you got lucky or followed some unclear road signs that read only: BEACH. But if you pulled off the county road on a whip, you'd find the neighborhood surrounding this strip of the riverbank coming alive in the summers. Families sat in their yards on nice days and folks would walk to and from the beach, carrying towels and floaties. It's an exceptional little place, a neighborhood built around a third space of the best kind.

The Catfish Bar is a feature of the St. Croix River that can be credited as the source of my hometown. It is a sandbar that extends into the river from Wisconsin. Before bridges or ferries, it served as a rare crossing point when the water levels were low. Without it, colonizers would not have chosen the site for the village that would eventually become Afton. The Catfish Bar is still visible today. Most of the summer, it's lined with boats and brimming with people. From the marina on the Minnesota side, you can swim to the Catfish Bar, but it's treacherous. There's a lot of boat traffic, and the current picks up where the sandbar ends. But I swam that crossing many times. I met rich friends whose parents had houseboats anchored there. Whenever I went out onto the water, the Catfish Bar was a destination, a gathering point, and a defining feature. This heap of sand has made this place for centuries, I'm sure.

Just north of downtown Stillwater is a commemorative park on the banks of the St. Croix River. Like something out of a Twain novel, it is complete with sandstone bluffs, a waterfall, walkways and trails, and the Stillwater Cave. As a child, I would stop at the Boom Site sometimes on kayak, or hike around with friends. The place traces its history to the logging boom that helped establish Stillwater. It was the spot where felled logs floating down the St. Croix River were linked together in what were called "booms" in the nineteenth century. Today a roadside plaque and local knowledge maintains this history.

Location: Oakland Junior High School, Lake Elmo, MN
Description: Through some of the most awkward and disorienting years of my life, I attended Oakland Junior High. I mark this place only to acknowledge its general significance to my time and development in those years. I wish I could say it was a good place to attend 7th to 9th grade, but I would be lying. Some of the teachers and staff were amazing, and I had good friends and so forth, but I struggled those years in ways I would prefer not to describe. Oakland Junior High did not make things easier for me. During my time there, I grew to resent parts of my education and my tweenish brain subsequently developed other priorities, none too healthy. I moved away from schoolwork and sports and started working at jobs that were not helpful, only necessary. I think some work experience is good at that age, but I ended up filling all my time outside school washing dishes, working in kitchens and on the riverboats, and spending any remaining time with friends. I tried other adult things too early, too. I lacked the kind of guidance I needed in those years, and part of those developments stemmed from this school, which was not a good one.

I think we often forget the size and scale of the infrastructure around us. In the US, we do this because we experience it by vehicle most of the time. We travel wide, long roads everywhere. We pass tall buildings, cross high bridges. All of it is made at the scale of cars. I don't usually think about such things in my day-to-day life, but I remember being conscious of these built environments and their misfigured scales when I was a child who wanted to cross the I-94 Bridge. This bridge connects the freeway over the St. Croix River. I lived on the Minnesota side. Sometimes, I would want to walk or bike to Hudson, the river town on the Wisconsin side, but this bridge was massive, busy. It felt unsafe. There was a narrow walkway along one edge with just a Jersey wall separating you from the speeding traffic. I never attempted to cross. If I had been able to, the river would not have felt like such a barrier to places in my life as a child, which is a shame, because Hudson had more things to do than my hometown. So, instead of a crossing, the bridge most often served as an overhang. If you head down the adjacent road, you'll pass underneath the bridge. From there, you'll see it's remarkable underbelly of steel and concrete in a long, parallel division over the water. The traffic echoes. My friends and I would meet up there sometimes, like teenage trolls. We liked it because it felt so hidden and unsupervised.

In the Afton village, there is a building that contains the post office and a few commercial spaces. Those spaces were constantly being filled and vacated in a rotation of small businesses that tried (and failed) to establish themselves in the smallness of Afton. When I turned 14––the age when I could first get a job––one of those businesses was Pizza Planet. It was a terrible pizza shop run by a retired prison guard who was crotchety and inept. I applied to be a dishwasher. It was my first "real job" besides babysitting or mowing lawns. A few of my friends were hired, too, and so I was excited and biked to work each day with glee. But soon the owner's sour demeanor became an issue. This compounded as the business failed to make a profit. We were just kids, but he took it out on us, going into fits of rage over the minutest of details. The whole venture didn't last longer than six months. When Pizza Planet closed, I remember being floored by the whole experience. I think it was the first time I realized that some adults had no idea what they were doing.

North of Afton is another river village called Bayport. It's small, maybe 5,000 people. There is one park on the shore and the rest is blockaded by private marinas and houses, and the Anderson Windows factory. Bayport also has the Stillwater prison atop the hill. The prison and the window factory keep Bayport's residents employed. It's quiet, working class. It was always a long, long bike ride to Bayport, but I did it occasionally because good friends lived there and we haunted the streets together in the summers and bummed around in basements and passed the time away with childish antics. It was a fun place for me, a good community of kids and a relatively safe town to walk about, unsupervised.

Once, when I was young, we drove to Taos, where family friends had a condominium. We stayed with them and skied Taos Valley. By then, I was pretty good at skiing. I had gone many times to the hills near my home in Afton. Taos Valley was the first mountain I ever descended, though. It was a revelation. I don't remember anything about the trip except the long chairlift ride, so long I couldn't believe it––and then the joy of a meandering pass that took twenty times as long as the hills I was familiar with back home. I think this early experience made me a lifelong skier. Those New Mexico peaks and the powdery snow were an environment that made me feel free. Many trips around the American West have followed, but sadly it has become an expensive hobby, and so I don't go on such trips anymore. I used to associate mountain skiing with natural wonder, like how Muir saw Yosemite. But now I associate it with yuppies. The problem is that corporate resort companies bought all the hills over the past two decades. Now most people––myself included––have been priced out of the sport.

The Afton House Inn is on the National Register of Historic Places. Along the few blocks that comprise the Afton village, it stands out with its white paint and cloudy windows. Inside, the old décor is maintained––creaky floors, lots of Victorian dining sets and daguerreotypes and doilies. I used to pass the inn on my bike almost every summer day as a child. Its old charm was lost on me then. Eventually, I got a job here as a dishwasher. I was fifteen. It was my second job, after washing dishes at Pizza Planet. I liked working in the kitchen because the staff and the chef treated me like an adult. They swore and drank and smoked. They were abrasive and cunning in ways so emblematic of kitchen staff. It was a poor environment for me, but I liked it then. I wanted to be edgy and charming like a cook. I should have paid more attention to the fixtures, the history adorning the walls. Maybe then today I'd remembered this place for its historic charm instead of its dirty kitchen.

On another family trip out West we ended up at the Snowbowl in Arizona. I remember the expansive views across the flatter plains near Flagstaff. The forests were all pine, the air far more dry than other places we had visited. The skiing was good. By that time, I could meander the hills all on my own, make my way without much supervision, and I distinctly remember doing so and meeting my folks back at the chalet after long days exploring the mountain by ski.

This was my public high school, home of the Ponies. It's a brick building with long corridors full of lockers, classrooms, children. It was a properly resourced public high school. We had a weight room, a theater, a football field. Behind the building were several acres of marsh that they billed as an environmental learning space. It served mostly white and middle-class teens like myself. Some of the teachers and staff were terrific. Others, not so much. For my part, I wasn't a spectacular student back then. In those days, I skated through my education on whatever paths of least resistance I could find. I was more concerned with my jobs outside of school––working at the Afton House Inn or the Stillwater Riverboats. I think most adults at the time saw me as a punk kid who was destined for working class life, and so I lived up to that expectation. But I regret my approach to high school now. I think I could have gotten much more out of it. I also think I would have flourished at a less conservative, more diverse place. Although I didn't have the language to articulate it back then, I could still sense that my values were not entirely in line with the small town conservatives who ran the school. They had a habit of pigeonholing students, myself included. I thought more creative freedom and opportunity was better.

One of the defining aspects of my young adulthood was the Stillwater Riverboats. They are a family-owned business with a catering branch, a banquet hall, and six riverboats with passenger capacities ranging from about 25 to 600 people. I worked for this company from ages 16 to 24. For the longest time, I thought it would be my only career. The family that owned the business gave me opportunities and trained me at a variety of tasks. I started as a dishwasher in their catering branch, but eventually became a senior deckhand. By my early twenties, I was being groomed to become a riverboat captain. I loved being on the river every day. I'd walk from bow to stern and supervise the buffets, assist the bartenders, handle security, and talk with the captains in the wheelhouse. On Sundays, they had a brass band that played classic river songs. I was also a crew member on trips to St. Louis for hull inspection––a monumental, month-long excursion. It would have been a very different life, had I chosen to stick with it and become a riverboat captain. But there were other things I longed for. I didn't want to work late evenings every summer, or drink after work all the time. It was a seasonal job. I'd forever need a second job in the winters. I didn't want to stay in my hometown forever, either, or stay poor my whole life. As beautiful as the river was, the reality of the work, and the hard future it came with, drove me away.

On another family roadtrip out West, we stopped to ski at Steamboat Springs in Colorado. This trip blurs in my memory with the other roadtrips and ski resorts, but I am certain we once skied here. I vaguely remember being mostly on my own on the hills. By this time, I was spritely and adept on skis, and I wanted to go faster, go on harder terrain. Steamboat Springs had night skiing, too, and so I stayed on the hills for long, long days on this trip, coming back to our little rental windswept and exhausted.

At Big Sky in Montana the the hills go up, up to a monumental peak. It was too daunting for me, to go to the top on that trip, but I remember wishing I was brave enough to do it. I still went to their next highest ledges, though, and challenged myself in some of the deepest snow I've ever encountered. I also remember the bowls––those wide faces of the mountain––where you could ski along the edge of the face for acres and acres, back and forth. This ski area deserves its prestige. The scale of the place, and its isolated nature, really make you feel like you're traversing untamed hills.

The Stillwater Riverboats owned the Grand Banquet Hall and Grand Pizza. It's a big, family-owned operation. I started working here as a dishwasher. Then a prep cook. Then I was plucked out of the kitchen and began working as a deckhand on the riverboats. For a long time, I thought I'd work for this company forever. I liked the banquet hall a lot. The kitchen catered for the riverboat excursions and weddings and all sorts of events in town. We used to clean thousands of dishes every day, just me and a few other kids my age. As a prep cook, I also learned to chop, dice, mix, process, and prepare fruit bowls, salads, seasoned meats, hors d'oeuvres, and desserts. Sometimes, I also stocked and ran items to the boats and other off-sight events. I learned to manage inventory for hundreds of patrons at a time. The chef was an excellent manager, a kind person who mentored his employees. He and the rest of the staff encouraged me. They gave me opportunities. I can still remember the kitchen, the walk-in coolers. The dish pit, just a humid, loud corner of the basement. We used to drive a repurposed U-Haul van back and forth from the banquet hall to the dock, bringing food to the masses on the riverboats. It seems a far cry from my life now, but for a long time, I thought this was it for me.

In almost every town in America, there's a Taco Bell that became a default meetup spot for teenagers on the weekends because it was open late, until 2AM. This was that Taco Bell for me. If you had a car, you could park in the parking lot and wait on any given Saturday night, and eventually friends would arrive, unprompted. We didn't have much else to do in those late hours. We'd order Crunch Wrap Supremes and talk and get into trouble. Sometimes, these meetups would grow into little parties with whole gangs of teenagers swarming around the parking lot. I'll refrain from too many details here, because it was not always good behavior, but it was surely memorable, at least, and it brought my little life as a teenager into a larger nexus of American experience in the 2000s––the broad consequence of one corporate decision to stay open late––creating a sort of universal teenage place at Taco Bell in those years.

Location: St. Croix Valley Recreation Center, Stillwater, MN
Description: The recreation center hosted high school hockey games, public ice-skating, and offseason practices for baseball and soccer. It had two ice rinks and a heated dome with astro-turf fields. I worked here after high school, a job referred to me by the local riverboat company (my employer during the summers). They had a contract with the city to staff the recreation center, a contract that gave employees like me the opportunity for year-round work. I used to run the cash register, clean up the stands, and run the batting cages. In the winters during college, I drove home to cover these shifts. After a while, I was trained to drive the Zamboni, too. I know there is a lot of hokey charm associated with Zamboni drivers, but honestly I hated that job. The hockey parents in Minnesota were horrible people. They cared so deeply about their peewee and squirt practices that they felt justified treating everyone poorly––not just ice arena employees, but also their own children. I saw a lot of kids get berated over hockey practice. And I often had to boot coaches off the ice when their time was up, which drew a lot of ire. But worst of all, this job took me away from my studies. I resented it, resented needing it to make ends meet.

This is where I earned a Bachelor of Arts in English and a minor in Creative Writing. I applied because some friends said they were attending. I didn't know what I was going to do after high school. I figured I would work and try to save money, but since friends were going, I applied––the only place I applied. When I got in, I suddenly felt a relief that surprised me. I had not consciously concluded then that I needed more in life than menial jobs, but that relief from a college offer was my first sign. I remember my parents driving me the two hours South down Highway 61. They moved me into Lourdes Hall and we took a picture together and then they drove off. On my first day in Winona, I biked and walked all over town. It was a place that felt so, so relieving. Yet also familiar. It was another river town, downstream and lush with wooded bluffs and old bridges and floodplains, a jewel in the Driftless Region. The campus had redbrick buildings and bustling crowds of peers. It was also small, small enough for me to get some mentorship from faculty, which I needed. All of my prior guidance came from family and employers who pictured a different life for me––a working class, consistent life. The simple life, the good life, unless you were like me. I always craved quiet spaces for thinking about hard things, and Winona offered that to me in a manageable portion at the start of my adulthood. It was not a big, prestigious university or anything like that, but it showed me that I could put my mind to work in place of my hands.

Lourdes Hall was my dormitory in my freshman year of undergrad. It had all the charm of an old college dorm. It was old, cold, expansive––yet no corner was private. The halls were tile, the doors clanking and heavy. The outer façade was brick and windows. I had two roommates who became good friends. I had a resident assistant who overlooked some dubious activities. There were gendered wings of the building that had everyone flustered. It even had tales of hauntings––the ghost of a nun whose baby had been thrown down the elevator shaft! It was spooky and fun. Although I was ready to get out of the dorm by the end of the first year, I always looked back on that experience fondly. It ensured I had community in my first year of college.

On weekends back home during college, I was accustomed to studying at the Stillwater Public Library. I went here before and after my shifts at work. It was just up the hill from the riverboats and not too far from the recreation center.  It was a good library. It had several floors, computers, study rooms, a balcony overlooking the town. Studying here saved me drives home during those long days when I had to cover shifts but also complete my schoolwork. I remember being exhausted here, in my work uniform, trying to finish papers. I wrote a lot of fiction here, too. If not for this public library, I wouldn't have been able to manage my jobs and academic responsibilities through those challenging, formative years.

Slippery's Bar was made famous from the 1990s film Grumpy Old Men. The bar has movie memorabilia all over the place––signed actor photos and props from the set. They play the film nonstop on a television in the corner. They host the Grumpy Old Men festival. It's the only notable thing in Wabasha. A kitschy, silly little business. I drove past this place many times on my trips home from college. I don't think I ever stopped on my own, but once or twice, when my dad was with me, we'd pull off the road and enjoy Slippery's garish references to an obsolete movie.

Lake City is the halfway point between Winona State University and my hometown. It's a beautiful place on Lake Pepin. Just off Highway 61, this Dairy Queen is where I would stop for a snack or a restroom break on my drives back and forth from college. There's nothing particularly notable about it. It's just like any other Dairy Queen; although, it's right on the edge of the lake and has a terrific view. But I mark it as a respite from those long hours when I was making my way back and forth weekly from my life as a college student to my life as a working young man, trying to juggle many things. If I made it to this Dairy Queen, I had accomplished the transition.

This library is the study hub of Winona State University. Oh, the hours I spent there! It's where I wrote papers and studied for exams. It's also where I hid away on many occasions, where I would go to decompress and excuse myself from social obligations. It was a respite sometimes from the craziness of undergraduate social life and my demanding jobs. I'd hide away at some table or study booth at the top floor, claim one of those nooks and crannies to cozy oneself into. I'd play chess online and study and read, for hours and hours, often late into the evenings. When I'd emerge from the library on those long days, I'd feel like my heart and brain had reset, and the perpetual grind of those years felt bearable again.

The Acoustic Café remains the best hoagie sandwich I've ever had. They sell footlongs with fresh ingredients and a signature Italian seasoned oil. They host music performances and keep a little lending bookshelf stocked. It is a good spot in the redbrick downtown of Winona. It was one of my favorite indulgences during my undergrad years, a stop by the Café to meet friends to study and enjoy a sandwich. I used to take dates here, too, and found it to be a good place for conversations. It was never too loud or crowded to hear your dates speak, and as far as inviting restaurants go in Winona, it was always one of the best options.

After our first successful family roadtrip to ski, my parents made it an annual event. Skiing was the one activity the whole family could do together––my mother, father, sisters, and I would load our winter wear into the family SUV and drive long, long trips out West. Our second took us all the way to Lake Tahoe. We stayed in a cheap motel and spent long days on those hills. They blur in my memory with all the mountain slopes we explored in those days, but one thing I remember about Lake Tahoe was the commemorative Olympic signage everywhere. Those colorful rings and the prestige of skiing somewhere that once had hosted the Olympics made me feel big.

My younger sister attended this university for a couple years before she transferred to the main campus in Minneapolis-St. Paul. I remember visiting her once for a long weekend. We explored the campus on the hill above Lake Superior. There were tunnels connecting the buildings to save students the trouble of walking outside in the bitter Minnesota cold. There was the rest of Duluth, its neighborhoods and forests. The blocks all around campus housed students in old houses, my sister included. It was just like Winona, but colder. On that trip, I helped my younger sister get settled into college right on the heels of our family collapsing. My mother was gone. My father was absent, and we did our best to support each other from across the state. On that visit, we spent a lot of time socializing with other college students on campus. It was a time to find some community and support as best we could, and I remember feeling like I had to survey the place for my younger sister, who would have otherwise been alone.

La Crosse is the larger city on this stretch of the river. It has a downtown, a regional airport. It wasn't often, but sometimes my friends and I would venture over and down the river to take part in some event that La Crosse had going for it. The best of those excursions was a Bob Dylan concert. It was a lot of fun, but his voice was shot after a national tour. La Crosse was the last place scheduled. Bob went out on stage looking ancient, moving slow like the old man that he was. He never got up from his seat the whole performance, and he sang without even trying to hold his notes. I didn't care, though. I was young and in that phase where I was obsessed with classic rock and old hippie music. He played all his folk hits and more. It made me feel connected to previous generations. It was an early revelation about the shortness of a decade, of a century. There I was in La Crosse, Wisconsin, a town that hadn't changed probably in 60 years, listening to the same musician that my parents would have enjoyed.

This cemetery is down the hill from where I grew up. It's the place where my mother is buried. She died suddenly from heart failure, a surprise to everyone. I remember those whirlwind weeks that followed her passing. They pulled me out of college and work and thrust me into a dissolving family where I tried my best to hold it all together. Then, just as quickly, I had to go back to my day-to-day life. Those were formative days. The gravity of this spot brings me back to that grief-stricken time. It wasn't just losing my mother, but a certain dynamic of our family which she held together. Life was harder in all things for many years because of it.

Location: Minnesota Marine Art Museum, Winona, MN
Description: This art gallery overlooks a chute off the main channel of the Mississippi River where barges are left empty and waiting. It has a prairie garden out front, tables and chairs, and a gorgeous view of the bluffs. The building looks like an old mill with windows and wood shingles. It's a spectacular place, but the greatest treasures lay inside. They have lake, marine, and river landscapes by the greatest painters of all time. They have works by Winslow Homer, Vincent Van Gogh, Pablo Picasso, Georgia O'Keeffe. For a small college town like Winona, it's a breathtaking and surprising collection. I used to go here alone in undergrad to refresh my soul, rest my heart, revitalize my mind. It was always quiet, never crowded. The art spoke to my love for the water. It's still my favorite art gallery in the world.

Off a busy county road you'll find Mickey's Diner, a classic diner with a flattop grill and cooking stations in front of a row of booths. It's got a big gravel lot and the Mississippi River behind it. This spot should not be confused with the other Mickey's Diner in downtown St. Paul. That one is good, too, but this one is the hidden gem, the little captured bit of mid-century Americana open 24 hours, serving cheap, delicious bacon and eggs, steaks, and pancakes. I would venture at late hours sometimes when I came home from college. It felt like going to the diners in the movies. The best restaurant experience you can have.

Target Field is the baseball stadium for the Minnesota Twins. I know major league baseball has some fine stadiums across the country, but in my opinion, Target Field is the best. Yet when it first opened in 2010, I was unsure how I'd feel. I grew up going to the Metrodome, an admittedly hideous building, but nonetheless nostalgic. But when I first stepped inside Target Field, I was struck by the Minneapolis skyline which almost looked like it was put in place for the field itself. The wide pathways under the stadium seats were clean and breezy. The patios at the entrances were welcoming, bright. The whole experience charmed me, and while I could never afford to go to games often, it was always a great experience––friends, conversation, a beautiful field and a slow game. My best memories of a casual baseball fan were here.

Off Highway 61 are winding roads up the coulees into the bluffs. The fields framed by this landscape are green, lush. It's the place Hamlin Garland wrote about, a geography carved slowly by water. It's quiet. Life is insulated. If not for the great river, there would be no sense of direction. I absolutely adore those lost roads into the hills. They lead to timeless, ancient places where fresh water comes from, where life hasn't changed. I found myself here visiting friends and mentors by my junior year of college. They showed me what life could be like––a life of the mind and one in tune with the rhythms of the nature of a place. And it was this place, a good place. They call it Minnesota City, but there's scarcely even a town. It's truly just the landscape of coulees and bluffs and farmhouses tucked away on gravel roads.

The Loft Literary Center is a nonprofit that supports literary initiatives and events in the Twin Cities. It's located in the Open Book, a warehouse converted to a literary sanctuary in the heart of Minneapolis. Milkweed Editions keeps its offices here. So does the Minnesota Center for Book Arts. After undergrad, I took creative writing classes at The Loft and continued to hone my craft. On those weekday evenings, I'd drive into the city, usually tired and a little nervous. But I was eager to take part in some creativity and community. At that time, it was hard to get evenings off from my various jobs. I was far too busy. And more each day, I felt removed from my education. But this place was a beautiful elevation of my interests at a time when I needed it most. With the creative work I improved here, I was able to apply to MFA programs, and those tired evenings paid off.

There was a time when I made pilgrimages to Loring Park, a peaceful, open space in the middle of a vibrant Minneapolis neighborhood. It's near the sculpture garden, the Walker Art Center. There's a pretty pond and good restaurants. After I completed my undergrad, I was no longer satisfied with the secluded reaches of the Twin Cities metro. I went inward, seeking culture and opportunity, and this park felt like an indulgence I could enjoy more often, if I pursued a different life. Those were restless years, the ones right after undergrad. I was becoming increasingly desperate to find higher purpose and escape those dead-end jobs.

Location: Tavern on Grand, St. Paul, MN
Description: The Summit Avenue neighborhood of St. Paul is one of the most charming places you'll find in the Midwest. Yet to experience the deepest depths of Minnesota culture here, you must go to Tavern on Grand for a walleye sandwich and cheese curds. It's the best walleye in the world!

Way out in the wildest parts of the American West, you'll find a ski hill near the borders of Idaho and Wyoming: Grand Targhee. It's not the largest or highest mountain. Nor is it posh or modern. It's a good old fashioned ski resort with just the mountains and the main chalet. I quite liked it. My family did, too. It was friendly terrain and offered spectacular views of the Grand Tetons. I would rank it among my favorite ski resorts––grand in its environment, but modest in its prices and accommodations. I think the best ski experiences bring you closer to nature. My memory of this tucked away resort feels very much this way.

In downtown Hudson there's this public library where I would go some evenings to write and study. This began not long after I finished my undergraduate degree. I had moved back home. I was taking as many shifts at the riverboats and the ice arena and the ski hill as I could manage, and looking for better jobs, too. But if I could squeeze in a free evening, I'd head to this library and find an open space near one of the windows overlooking the river, and I'd put my mind to work, writing. I wrote a lot of fiction back then. Short stories, vignettes, several unfinished novels. Eventually, I started working on grad school applications here. It's a place that helped me hang onto my academic interests in those two years after my undergraduate degree.

For a week during the summer after undergrad, my father and younger sister and I drove out West and stayed in a cabin near the Frying Pan River. It was the last family trip we ever took, and the only one we ever took after my mother passed away. I insisted we go. I think I sensed a need for it, a chance to find a way to be a family again without my mother around. I'm not sure how successful the trip was in that regard. By the fifth day, I resolved to hike up the mountain to Sawyer Lake, a body of water several acres wide, crystal clear and full of trout. I went alone. The hike was especially difficult and so my dad and sister were not eager to join. I wore myself out horribly on that hike. The elevation and the length of it were intense. But the view of the lake, with trout jumping and the last jagged peak behind it, stays with me. Up there, I was suddenly happy to be alone.

After undergrad, I was working a lot, trying to cobble together some semblance of financial stability. I was also desperate for change and tired. Eventually, I couldn't take it anymore, and so I squeezed some days off into my schedule and drove West to ski in the mountains. Breckenridge was the first place I went. Then Keystone, then Vail. At the time, I had an employee pass from working the chairlifts at Afton Alps, the local ski resort near my home that Vail Corporation had purchased in the 2000s. Still, I spent way too much money between the drive and lodging and food. I remember it fondly, but looking back I can tell it was a bad financial decision. My last big ski trip.

Barker's was the bar of choice for my close-knit friends during those years after college when I was still at home. It's in an old brick building on the main drag in Hudson, Wisconsin. The fresh-cut fries are spectacular. Most everything else about this place is what you would expect from a small town bar. I remember feeling grown up for having a preferred place to frequent back then, but I also felt its inertia. To this day, if I go back to Barker's, everything remains the same. The booths, the bar stools. The people working there. Time passes in one direction there, and not much can change your trajectory, if you stay too long.

My senior year of undergrad, a group of enthusiastic classmates and I formed Winona State University's first creative writing club. I was elected the Activities Coordinator. It was the most involved I ever felt as a student. We applied for a grant in the English Department to fund a trip to the Association of Writers and Writing Programs conference (AWP). With the funds secured, about a dozen of us drove to Chicago. We stayed in a dumpy motel and took the Blue Line to the convention center each day. I was enthralled. Chicago was the first big city I ever explored as a young adult. And it was my first exposure to a larger writing community and graduate programs. I wasn't immediately confident that I could fit in, but the experience stuck with me enough to apply to MFA programs a couple years later. On that trip, I also bummed around Chicago with my peers and it all felt like bigger things, further sights, greater possibilities. Much of the story of my twenties traces its roots to this trip to Chicago and AWP.

I remember my first time exploring the Riverwalk through the heart of Chicago. This place is a masterfully crafted landscape of fresh water, steel, and glass. It charmed me in my early twenties, charms me every time I go back. The first time, I walked along its sidewalks and bridges with a group of fellow college students, our necks craned upwards most the time. The weather, unusually warm for late February. We walked what felt like miles, and I could not believe I had been missing this kind of city experience my whole life.

Off I-80 in central Nebraska, there used to be a life-size tyrannosaurus rex that towered over the freeway. The sign next to it read: "Dinosaur Museum" and nothing more. On one road trip out West, I decided it was time to investigate. I took the exit and followed the signs. In a lone warehouse behind a gas station, the self-proclaimed Dinosaur Museum stood like something out of the Twilight Zone. It was surrounded by corn fields. No other businesses, homes, or structures, just a windowless warehouse with a backlit sign and a Phillips gas station. Inside, the lobby was supervised by an apathetic teenager. There were turnstiles. I paid for a ticket and entered the museum. It was endless rooms full of replica dinosaurs––life-size, like Jurassic Park––and fossils and dioramas. There were placards with information about all the species. No one else was there. At the end of the exhibit, there was a mirror maze. I have no idea why. To this day, it remains my favorite museum experience. The best museums, I think, are ones that make you feel like you've made a discovery. This place was that discovery in-and-of-itself. It was so random and so isolated that it was bound to feel that way. I wish it was still there. But no, I've checked. It closed down and the roadside t-rex was taken away.

DRC is a standardized testing and data company. They administer and grade standardized tests. Most of their work involves contracts with state-level education departments across the country. It was my first corporate job, and my last. I was a Scoring Supervisor. The work was both analytical and interpersonal. I had to complete what were called "calibration" exercises to keep graders working in coherent fashion. I also had to monitor their scoring trends over days, weeks, months. I think that's all I can legally say about the job. I'll only add that I quit the first chance I could. I did well there, but the business model repulsed me. Still, it was tough to go. It was the best pay I had ever received and it had a regular 9 to 5 schedule. But there were no opportunities to grow. I'd be monitoring scoring trends and pestering graders forever. And in the evenings and weekends, I still kept my other seasonal jobs and tried to save as much money as possible. The whole time, I was desperate to escape. I dreamed of going back to school.

We steered day and night, the crew of six, taking shifts and never stopping, for weeks, until we could do no more. That's when we docked on the levee in Hannibal and spent an evening in town. It was the only time we left the riverboats save when we reached our destination. Hannibal is the childhood home of Mark Twain. There's a statue of him behind a steering wheel on the bank. There are museums and gift shops full of all sorts of Twain iconography. We were tired, cranky. It was hard to sleep on that trip and the night shifts seemed to take ages. Once on shore, we drank too much. The locals received us with great fanfare. They were probably used to large crowds off the riverboats and they may have been disappointed that it was just the six of us, but they hosted us just the same. We were joined by a group of young hipsters who were sailing down the river. We were accompanied by some old-timers who guided us from bar to bar. On that months' long trip up and down the Mississippi River, the stop in Hannibal was exactly what it should have been: a respite, a romantic adventure steeped so completely in the imagination of the Father of Waters.

This is the location of one of my greatest failures. On that monumental trip for hull inspection, we steered day and night, nonstop, through fog and rain and barge traffic. Although I had worked for the riverboats for years, I hadn't much experience steering them. One night––it must have been 3AM––I was alone in the wheelhouse, approaching Lock & Dam 13. I was deliriously tired. The captain had descended to the kitchen for a snack. I was trying my best to focus on the upcoming lock, but somehow I managed to lose sight of the channel. I ran aground in shallow water maybe a mile North of the dam. The massive boat rumbled. It was the Avalon, a four story tall riverboat, and over 100 yards long. Mud kicked up in the water like crazy. It woke the whole crew.  We were otherwise fine but that's because I got lucky. It was a sandy spot. Had there been more jagged rocks under the water, I could have punctured the hull. I was anguished. I was the youngest and least experienced person on that trip. The crew didn't blame me––I had no business steering alone, especially not at night. But I wanted to succeed on that trip, and it was nearly a disaster. Afterwards, I kept up in my duties but remained hesitant about steering. The crew didn't trust me to steer after that, either. I was supervised for the rest of the journey.

Here in Alton, Illinois, just North of St. Louis, is a massive shipyard. It's where we completed hull inspection. We stayed on the riverboats in the heart of the shipyard while they were lifted out of the water. It was a loud place, a bright place. Shipyard workers kept busy at all hours. The river traffic here was relentless, too. Barges like space ships travelled through the channel, their giant spotlights casting blinding beams in search of red and green buoys. Tow boats whipped around the docks. The water was surely contaminated with all sorts of industrial residues. We probably spent two weeks here in total, a week per boat, waiting for the work to be done. It was a much needed break from navigating the Upper Mississippi River, but it was no break from each other. We watched movies, played cards, bummed around. Waited. Drank. We went to the local bars and hammed it up with the shipyard workers. We were restless here.

Location: Fast Eddie's Bon Air, Alton, IL
Description: The riverboat crew and I became regulars at Fast Eddie's while stuck at the shipyard. It's a popular bar in Alton where shipyard workers and barge deckhands and other river folk go. Some wandering souls from St. Louis would show up, too. There was a big tent for outdoor seating, incredible grilled foods––shrimp, burgers, brats. cheap drinks, too. We'd go here and drink and talk just for the change of scenery. The company didn't mind paying for these outings because the food was so cheap. The crowds didn't mind us, either. We fit in. We stayed for long periods because we had nothing else to do.

Once, while stuck at the shipyard in Alton, the riverboat crew and I went to the Argosy Casino to kill some time. The Argosy is a riverboat permanently docked on the banks of the Illinois side of the river. It has structures wrapping around it, walkways and adjacent restaurants and lobbies. If I remember correctly, the whole design is a gambling law loophole. There can be no casinos on land, but it's perfectly legal to gamble on the water in Illinois. We tried the buffet and slots and drank. There wasn't much else to it. But the novelty of a riverboat casino was a lot of fun. It was a bizarre and kitschy spot.

The locks and dams on the Upper Mississippi River are some overlooked infrastructure. Some are small and relatively benign. Others, though, are more substantial than any other buildings or features for miles around. Lock & Dam 19, for example, is a behemoth structure. The dam stretches across a wide portion of the river. On its northern side stands the Keokuk electric power plant, a brick edifice that seems to float on the water. The lock descends several hundred feet. It is quite the experience, to dock into the lock and feel the concrete walls rise above you. Those walls look down upon the top decks of the tallest riverboats when the water is drained. On my trips to St. Louis by river, I passed through this lock four times, and each time, it felt like being risen and lowered out of a massive grave.

Once, on the last trip back up the river from St. Louis, we had to tie up in Levee Park because the fog was so thick. From the bow of the riverboat, you could see maybe ten feet in front of you. It was a cold, pervasive fog that lasted all morning. Up this far North on the river, the channel is narrow and hazardous. One misstep and we could have run aground, stuck until a tow boat could be procured from somewhere far downstream. Levee Park saved our nerves that night. I remember approaching with radio in hand, trying desperately to spot the cleats to tie up, and guiding the captain who couldn't see a damn thing from up in the wheelhouse. Those slow-motion tense moments were frequent on those trips. But we managed to get tied up that night, and by early morning, the fog finally passed.

In the Spring of 2014, I flew to Seattle to attend the Association of Writers and Writing Programs conference. I had finished the riverboat journeys and I was back to my God-awful routine of work at several places––Data Recognition Corporation, the recreation center, and the ski hill. I had never been to Seattle. I went alone. I went because I missed the creative writing communities I had forged in undergrad. The trip corresponded with my MFA application cycle, too. I had been waitlisted at a couple programs, but hadn't gotten an acceptance letter yet. This fact––coupled with my desperation to escape my hometown––made the conference especially challenging. I felt inadequate. I feared speaking with people in case they were affiliated with some MFA program I hadn't heard back from yet. All the panelists and people at the booths were living their creative lives and I was only wishing I could. Yet the trip was still fruitful. Despite my uneasy feelings, I left only more assured of my desires to be a writer. And things worked out. I also came to love the city of Seattle. I met with my cousin who lives there and he showed me around. I stayed at a nice hotel, too, near the convention center, spending too much money, but deeming it worthwhile since I worked so much back home.

The SAM in Seattle is a spectacular art gallery. It proved a nice break from the conference, a place to kill some time and refresh my mind. I remember putting on my headphones, listening to music while I walked as slowly as I could through the galleries. On that weary trip, I managed to keep myself going by taking slow breaks at places such as this.

Is there a better market anywhere? I doubt it. Pike Place is that iconic Seattle fish market with the workers who toss the fish, stack the fish, sell the fish. There are many good restaurants, too, and cafes that overlook the Puget Sound. Wandering the market was one of my favorite experiences in Seattle. I bought fresh fish and shipped them home. I enjoyed the showmanship of the market workers and the diversity of shops. This place is enough to make anyone fall in love with Seattle. It's what every city should be built around.

Down a long corridor of Pike Place Market is this little café with spectacular views of the Puget Sound. I'd come here each morning before the AWP conference and I'd eat some assortment of bagels, salmon lox, orange juice, bacon and eggs. I'd journal and stare off pensively, trying to look interesting, trying to feel creative and inspired. I quite enjoyed the spot.

Location: University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV
Description: I completed my MFA at UNLV's Creative Writing International Program. It was probably the best thing that ever happened to me. It pulled me out of my insular little world in Minnesota and plopped me in the heart of a wonderful, creative city. And the study abroad requirements sent me further still. I dedicated three years to becoming a better writer. I started a teaching career, too. I made lifelong friends, developed new interests and hobbies. It was an excellent program. I grew up at UNLV in many ways, as an artist, intellectual, and citizen. And so the place stays with me. The campus, a desert garden with tastefully designed structures. The student body, diverse, talented, gregarious. UNLV is in the heart of the city. The Vegas skyline and the mountains frame the view. I miss the creative writing community. I miss my naive excitement about what it all meant and the unbounded sense of potential that I felt living here. I miss the faculty. My advisor, Doug Unger, was a gentle, brilliant writer, a gardener of a mentor, too, who planted ideas and let them grow.

Lied Library is UNLV's main library. It's several stories of open space and bookshelves and study tables. I used to meet with friends here, complete coursework or grade. Through teaching, I also came to know the librarians who were liaisons to undergraduate classes. Those librarians serve the UNLV community exceptionally well. They were a model of service for academic libraries. I learned a lot about the field through them. Plus, the space––it's just an excellent built environment with uniquely designed areas and a range of accommodations. I always enjoyed being here. It was bustling but peaceful.

Cugino's was located between my first apartment in Las Vegas and the UNLV campus. It was an authentic New York-style pizza parlor. The owners were transplant New Yorkers who clearly cared about the quality and tradition of their cheese pizzas. They had the parmesan and pepper at each table. They had glass bottles of coke for sale. The pizza was excellent–thin and cheesy but not too greasy and crispy crust but never burnt. I used go here with my MFA friends or I'd get a pizza delivered on special occasions. It's where I learned about true NY-style pizza which remains my favorite kind.

The Arts Factory is a community center with pop-up stores and galleries, a bar, and an event space. I did some public readings here during my MFA program. The first was in my first semester and I was mortified, but it went well. It was a good spot, a much needed local art venue in Las Vegas. The MFA crowd would gather here often. I liked it because, if I got tired of the conversations, I could always slip away and peruse the arts and gallery scenes. And then, once the group was ready, we'd be off to other parts of downtown.

Early in my MFA program, the Writer's Block opened and became the spot for public readings and literary events. It was primarily a bookstore, but it had a seating area in the back. We held our Neon Lit series here––a chance for MFA students and visiting writers to read their work. It was always cram-packed. I get ill from public speaking, but I did it often here anyway. Across the street was Atomic Liquors. It's where we'd go after the readings. And then, all of downtown Las Vegas. The whole of Fremont Street was a lively joy. Years later, though, the Writer's Block moved into a new building. It became part of a major non-profit in Las Vegas, occupying a lobby space in a grander literary center. Kudos to them, but I'll always miss the little building downtown where I shared my creative work with others.

Atomic Liquors was the bar of choice for the creative writing crowd (especially the poets). It was across the street from the Writer's Block, a small bookstore and venue where we held public readings. It was also at the end of Fremont Street. We'd start here, then disperse across the lively neon happenings of downtown Las Vegas. I liked Atomic Liquors but it wasn't my favorite spot. It was loud and disorienting sometimes. I've never liked crowded bars. But I'd stop by sometimes. There was always someone there from the MFA crowd.

Location: Bellagio Piano Bar, Las Vegas, NV
Description: In the lobby of the Bellagio sits a fancy piano bar. It's expensive, ritzy. The pianists are talented. I used to go here for a drink to splurge with friends. One drink was splurging enough. It's no secret place. It's right there in the lobby, but it feels like being in a different social class altogether, when you go the piano bar for a cocktail.
