I once travelled a large stretch of the Upper Mississippi River, from Stillwater, Minnesota, to St. Louis, Missouri. I went as a crew member on the Stillwater Riverboats. It was not a leisurely excursion. We transported two massive boats to St. Louis for hull inspection––a mandatory task supervised by the US Coast Guard. St. Louis was the closest place with dry docks big enough to lift the Majestic Star and the Avalon out of the water. Both vessels could carry over 300 people. But on these trips, it was just a crew of six. We took one after the other, up and down the river twice in a two-month period. It was at the end of the summer season and we barely made it back, the river almost closed up on us. We were breaking ice in the final days. It was one of the greatest adventures of my life to date. For 24 hours a day, for weeks on end, I lived on a riverboat and I saw the great northern half of the river in Autumn. It's beautiful. Bluffs, chutes and beaches, colorful trees and shrubs. Some parts narrow, creating rapid currents, while at the locks and dams the river always widens. Those massive floodplains are the harbingers of life. Carved through them is the designated channel. It takes a keen eye to follow the red and green buoys and share the channel with the barges which stack themselves in long lines, longer than football fields. They move slowly with one large spotlight scanning the water like some kind of seeking god. The river remains my favorite landscape. You can't feel any other way after seeing it as I have.

Glenwood Springs is a town beyond the highest peaks of the Rockies. On my many drives out West along I-70, I'd stop here before or after traversing the treacherous pass to Denver. The pass goes through tunnels, mountain tops, and ski resorts. If it snowed heavy, you could get stuck for hours. That's why I always stopped in Glenwood Springs––a sign you'd made it through, if you were headed West. Or, if you were headed East, a chance to prepare with fuel, snacks, and by checking the weather. It's a touristy little town. They have cave tours and hot springs. There's a gondola. I vaguely remember doing a cave tour on one stop, but otherwise it was just a place to ease the strain of long journeys.

From here, on the highway heading toward Las Vegas, the city lights first become visible over the horizon. If you're ever taking this drive down I-15, time it so you're driving at night. You'll be heading South through basins in the darkness of the desert with only the headlights on the road. The ranges to your left and right will shroud the night sky, but then you'll come around this bend, right here. At that moment, press play on Elvis's "Viva Las Vegas" and let the grand show begin with all its brightness and vivacity across the entire Las Vegas Valley. This will recreate in some ways my experience arriving at this place in a U-haul, carrying my hope for a new and better life. It's a whole view of the city as it wants to be seen. It's a dreamscape, a wildly adventurous view of America's most enigmatic city.

The Brooklyn Bowl is a club, music venue, and bowling alley. I went to a few concerts here, always feeling displaced. It was small potatoes compared to other event centers in Las Vegas, but it was a lot for me. I liked the ambiance. I liked the hybridity of the space. Yet loud, crowded places always give me the heebie jeebies. I have a degree of ochlophobia. Still, I went on various invitations to the Brooklyn Bowl over the course of my time in Las Vegas, trying to fit in, wanting a touristy experience. I'm glad I did. It was always an adventure.

The High Roller is a massive Ferris Wheel permanently constructed near the Las Vegas Strip. Its platforms fit nearly two-dozen people apiece. Up it goes, above most of the highrise casinos. Each platform has a bar with exhorbitantly expensive drinks. When I lived in Las Vegas, a strange thing began to happen: people, acquaintances, friends from back home would always reach out to me if or when they were in town, seemingly without pretense. But they usually wanted company, a familiar face. I began to deduce that they wanted someone to break the ice of the whole Las Vegas experience. The city can be intimidating. There's so much to do. I eventually formed a little routine, like a tour guide. I'd always meet folks near the High Roller and suggest we'd go for a spin. It was cheap, as long as you didn't buy the drinks, and it usually matched the expectations of people's big dreams for their Las Vegas vacation. I have good memories from that giant contraption.

The MGM Grand is a major casino on the Las Vegas Strip. When I first moved to Las Vegas, I ended up here fairly often with friends or visitors. I went to Ka, the Cirque de Soleil show. I practiced blackjack. It was the first casino I became familiar with, mainly because of its central location just down the road from UNLV. It's not my favorite casino, but it's a good one.

Oh, SW, a wonderful old haunt of mine. You can't really go wrong with any of the steakhouses in Las Vegas. They are all expensive and good. So, too, is SW, but what sets it apart is the lagoon just outside with a patio and a cascading fountain twenty feet high. At 7pm each night, the fountain comes alive with an animatronic frog that crawls over the top. It sings Louis Armstrong songs. There is no warning, no explanation. It goes on while you enjoy your dinner. It makes you believe that anything can happen in Vegas.

Stake Out was the 24-hour bar near my first apartment in Vegas. It was also the place where MFA folks would go to write or workshop sometimes. It was a relatively quiet bar. Like most bars in Vegas, you could smoke inside. The food was good. It was lazily themed around classic film, just some old movie posters. Upstairs, they had cheap pool tables. You could go there with your laptop and a pack of smokes and sit in one of the booths and write and look interesting. It was the kind of bar where people brought novels to read. It was the kind of bar where you could be unbothered, my favorite kind.

Shortly after returning from the AWP conference in Seattle, I got good news: I was accepted to to two MFA programs in Creative Writing! And suddenly my dreams were coming true. I decided to attend the International Program at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. Within a month, I found myself driving out West to find housing and to meet some folks from the program. Denver was the halfway point on that long drive. Over subsequent years, I ended up making that drive and ending up in Denver probably a dozen times. On the first trip, I drove with a former professor's husband, an enigmatic man who offered to carpool with me while he visited a sibling in Southern California. Denver was a relief. The drive across the Great Plains goes on and on and on. Then comes Denver, with its bright buildings and those big mountains on the horizon, proving you were actually heading somewhere. We didn't stay in Denver on that first trip. We drove right through. But on later visits, I'd stay a day or two and enjoy the crunchy culture and the cowboy attitudes. Denver is a transplant city. Lots of folks come for opportunity, seasonal adventures, a change in lifestyle. When you visit, you can't avoid imagining what it would be like to live there.

Brian Head is a true gem. It's one of the rare affordable ski resorts out West. It's small in comparison to other Utah resorts, but the snow is good and it's affordable and not nearly as crowded. There are few steep runs, but mostly easy terrain. It's a good place for older skiers or newbies. I went once with my dad when he visited me in Las Vegas. It was the last time I'll ever ski with him (he's no longer physically able). We enjoyed the runs, the views. It was a quiet weekend dedicated to the hills. We didn't realize it was the last time we'd ski together, but somehow the trip went exactly how we would have done it, if we had known. Just skiing, taking our time, enjoying every run that we could.

Once, on whim, two friends and I hopped in the car on a weekend and drove to Los Angeles. We made plans as we drove and dreamed big and agreed easily on our adventure. One of our activities was a John Williams concert with the Los Angeles Philharmonic at the Hollywood Bowl. I'll never forget the movie tunes done perfectly, the crowd swinging light sabers and cracking Indiana Jones whips and roaring with applause to the Jurassic Park theme. The Hollywood Bowl is a magical venue. It's a deep amphitheatre in the hillside where in the distance you can see the Hollywood sign. The weather was California perfect. Dry, warm, crisp. There is nowhere else I could imagine seeing that show.

Location: Student Recreation & Wellness Center, Las Vegas, NV
Description: This is the student gym at UNLV. When I first moved to Las Vegas, I didn't know anyone. I meandered about, lonely and a little shocked after such a big move. To keep my spirits up, I started going to the gym and exercising. I ran the track on the top floor where the skyline of the city spread itself across the windows. I started lifting weights in a serious way. Then I got to know some people in my MFA cohort. It was fortuitous that some of them––the ones who became my closest friends––were also weight lifters. We bonded and spent many days here at the gym. I got into the best shape of my life. I developed healthier habits. I stopped drinking and smoking. I owe this gym a lot in terms of my physical and mental health. It was one of the best parts of my life at UNLV. I know some folks associate college gyms with toxic culture and vanity, but frankly, I think those associations are wildly off. UNLV's gym was a supportive space for good healthy habits, a place where fitness was fun. The weight room was always full of all sorts of people––students, faculty, community members. It was a great equalizer, a melting pot of the Vegas crowds.

Location: Park on Fremont, Las Vegas, NV
Description: Park on Fremont is a strange little bar. It was my favorite bar in Vegas. They had excellent fries. The décor was strange, like cottagecore meets taxidermy meets macabre. The back patio was delightful, too. While sometimes crowded, it was never too loud, and outside, the downtown reveries and adventures always seemed to be waiting. I remember joining small groups here, closer-knit groups who arrived from every direction, came from every place across the country. We made a little home at this bar, relaxing together after full days of teaching and reading and writing.

Sunset Park is a large area with walking paths, volleyball, soccer fields, baseball fields, and a large pond. It's centrally located in the valley and quite popular. One thing folks don't usually know about Las Vegas is that it has exceptional public parks. This one was a common destination for pickup soccer games, dates, and MFA luncheons. I have memories at this park from throughout my time in Las Vegas.

There used to be a Staples store at this very spot, but it's since been demolished. I worked there for one summer–the summer of hell. I ran out of money and I needed a job. Staples was the first place that hired me. I worked in the Copy & Print Center. The pay was terrible. I had to donate plasma to get by as well. The work was also terrible. People would come in with major printing projects, expecting them to be done immediately. They were rude, impatient. The numerous pieces of equipment were complicated and finicky. The training was bad. One supervisor was big on role-playing customer service interactions. It was cringy... My other supervisor was a hardware savante but could not communicate any of his knowledge. The job was also corporate. We were forced to say, "My pleasure" to every customer. Part of my training also involved sitting in a closet with a desktop computer for eight hours, watching training videos, many of which were about rejecting union organizers. I quit as soon as the summer ended.

One summer during my MFA, I ran out of money. The graduate program didn't fund us well enough. We were left to make ends meet in the summers. I took a job at Staples, but it wasn't enough. I had to donate plasma twice a week here at Octapharma. It was a dystopian experience. Located in a neglected part of the city, Octapharma had lines of people out the door every day. Desperate people. The wait was usually three hours. Then they'd stick you and pay you on a cash card afterwards. All manner of mental health crises took place in that line. The staff was callous. I would leave feeling dizzy, exhausted, but with money to buy groceries. It was the thing that kept me afloat for those dire months.

A short drive West of Las Vegas, near the border of Nevada and California, is the Pioneer Saloon. It's a picturesque Old West place in the desert village of Goodsprings. It's been there for over a century, the place of hauntings, shootouts, cowboys. The MFA crowd would go there sometimes on the weekends for karaoke. I loathe karaoke, but I went for the experience of the place. I have fond memories of the cool nights with bar food and drinks. It's worth a stop, if you're ever in the area.

Location: Triple George Grill, Las Vegas, NV
Description: A longstanding steak and cocktail spot in downtown Las Vegas. I loved it, especially for power lunches. Not that I was ever rich or refined enough to need a business power lunch, but I could pretend occasionally here. It's affordable. The design is classic. The food is good. For someone like me who is sensitive to background chatter, it's also great because there are numerous closed booths and corners. It is a gem in Vegas, a local favorite.

Location: Red Rock Canyon, Las Vegas, NV
Description: West of Las Vegas is Red Rock Canyon, a conservation area full of hiking trails and rock formations. It is a destination for rock climbing, too, but I never went to climb. I'd go with friends or dates or take visitors to see the canyon and hike some of the trails. It's gorgeous. The tan, beige, red, and brown desert crumbles up out of the hillsides. The trails cut through sage brush, cacti, and yucca. There are herds of wild donkeys descended from the earliest ranchers in the area. It is a special place so close to a vibrant city. Because of Red Rock Canyon and the other parks and reserves in the area, my sense of place in Las Vegas is one far more natural in splendor than the usual cultural imaginings of the city. It has an abundance of natural treasures.

The Association of Writers and Writing Programs conference was in Minneapolis in 2015. I was an MFA student in Las Vegas at the time. We were funded for conference travel and so I went with friends and we stayed in my childhood home and commuted to the conference each day. It was the best AWP experience of the many I've attended. We worked the UNLV program's booth as MFA students for part of each day, but then meandered together through the book fair, to panels, to all sorts of things, and I got to play host in the evenings. It was a lot of fun.

My dad came to visit me once in Las Vegas. I took him to the Hoover Dam. It's the kind of thing he'd like. Structure, scale, concrete. We looked over the top of that behemoth slab and enjoyed the desert heat. Some of my best photos with him are from that day. It's worth a visit, the dam–one of the many unique attractions in and around Las Vegas.

I once drove straight to the coast from Las Vegas. I ended up on Venice Beach. It was exactly as the movies make it. It's strange, but there are few times when an imagined place turns out to be exactly as you expect it. Venice Beach is exactly as you would expect–lots of beautiful people, lots of activity, lots of music and vibes like a cool beach in the movies.

I once got lost in the Getty Museum. It's a massive compound on the hilltop. It's like a Bond villain's lair; although, brighter and more welcoming. It's one of my favorite stops any time I'm in Los Angeles.

Location: Golden Gate Bridge, San Francisco, CA
Description: I've been to San Francisco several times, but one of the most memorable trips was punctuated by a convertible ride over the Golden Gate Bridge. It's a beautiful structure with a wide view of the bay. A lighthouse and park stand at the end. There's a calmness to it, a calmness uncommon among scenes of such large scale. You would expect it to be sublime, but no–the bridge and the bay are serene.

Chinatown is a spectacular part of San Francisco. The architecture all tight together seems unchanged, a century of culture stacked atop itself and full of life. It's one of the best enclaves in America. I have forgotten the restaurant, but there was a place here that had the best Chinese food I've ever tasted. If ever I'm in San Francisco, I try to stop in Chinatown for the food and the exprerience.
If ever there was whimsy in urban design, it was epitomized by Lombard Street, that curvy, steep descent. I'm glad it exists, but I'm also glad it is a unique feature, not a common one.

I was once someone's date to a wedding on the Stanford campus. It was held in the Memorial Church, a stunning place at the center of the university. It has spectacular arches and frescos, stained-glass windows and mahogany pews. It's a remarkable thing to see on a secular campus. The students biked around outside on that sunny day. The ceremony was pleasant. I was charmed by Stanford, but I certainly felt out of place.

Location: San Gregario Beach, San Gregario, CA
Description: I once watched the sunset here across the horizon of the Pacific, painting the sky and the waters deep shades of red. I stood at the precipice of a tall cliff ledge over the sprawling, sandy beaches. I let the grave of our day spread itself behind me. Then I went back to the car, drove to the place I was staying, and ate a delicious meal.

The City Lights bookstore is a historic place founded by Lawrence Ferlinghetti. It has its own imprint, too, most famously publishing Allen Ginsberg's Howl. If ever there was a bookstore to visit, it would be City Lights. It is just plain good. Shelves, rows, nooks, corners to explore. And a rich history, a bookstore embodying San Francisco culture.

Above Salt Lake City, up a winding mountain road, are some of the best ski resorts in the world. My favorite has always been Solitude. It's fairly expensive, but not like other world-class ski resorts. It's a challenging mountain, but after years of skiing all over the West, I've come to find that Solitude matches my preferred level of difficulty. There are lots of long descents, some steep and foreboding, others leisurely and fine. I once went here for a long weekend during my MFA and quietly enjoyed the serene mountain views. The chalets are simple, cozy. The lifts on quiet days are none too crowded. It doesn't feel quite so commercialized like other resorts out West. If I could afford it, I'd probably ski here every winter. It's a good place.

Near the end of my MFA program, our favorite event space and bookstore caught a windfall: the Black Mountain Institute, a literary non-profit, elevated the bookstore and helped it relocate into a new arts center. The new location became a central hub for all the artists and cultured folks of Las Vegas. They have good coffee, good books. It's a charming, modern space–one that displays the power of benefactors, of the mega-wealthy, wielding their power through non-profits (in this case, for good).

Downtown Las Vegas is punctuated by the Fremont Street Experience––several blocks of casinos, shops, and restaurants covered by a lit archway and only accessible to pedestrians. It's a true menagerie complete with street performers and music every day of the year. I always told tourists to go there for cheaper options than the Las Vegas Strip. It's where locals usually chose to hang out. I once rode the zip line across the Fremont Experience. Many times, I walked those wild blocks on dates or nights out with friends. It was more my speed. It felt like a small town but with big energy, an environment encouraging you to shed all introversion and let live.

Tucked around this shopping mall was my favorite sushi restaurant in Las Vegas. Always packed for dinner, Sakana had an ambiance of joy and excitement. I'd go here for all-you-can-eat sushi on special occasions. I highly recommend.

There is a secret oasis in the desert if you take a county road from the highway down into the valley. You will be floored by the sheer greenery and the warmth of Moapa Valley between desert peaks. There is a dry riverbed that fills up sometimes, passes its runoff into the brush, and brings the valley to life. There are houses, ranches, people sparsely populating the area. The road takes you into the Valley of Fire where red and beige formations climb to the sky.

Antelope Canyon is a slot canyon in the Navajo Tribal Park. The tribe hosts tours of the canyon where they funnel you in, hike you up, and stop at various points to let you get totally Instagram-worthy photos. I went here once with a friend. It was a fun experience. Sort of strange, there were tons of people herded into the canyon, but it was good.

One time, when I was in love, I drove from Las Vegas to Dana Point for a long weekend on the beach, in the town, for quiet and privacy. It's a good place for it, if you can ignore the cookie cutter houses and the yuppy smarm. The beach and scenery are exactly as California wants to be seen. There's a marina, green but dry hills, a sunshine that never lets up. It's one of many charming coastal towns in California that all seem to blur together in my memory.

In the hills of Valparaiso stands a colorful, irregular polygon, the former home of Pablo Neruda. It's a museum now. I visited during a weekend in Valpo and it was a charming experience. All of the rooms were small, intimate. He was a tiny little man who liked to sit close to his guests, to huddle together near windows with expansive views. He used to walk every day through the streets of Valparaiso. His house and his spirit largely define the city, Pablo Neruda, the genus loci of the place. I loved it.

Valparaiso is famous for its colorful elevators that lift you up from the shore to the hillsides where restaurants, shops, and alleyways are full of adventure. The Ascensor Cordillera is one such elevator. It's a historic monument. It's over a century old. Still works. I rode it to save myself the walk up the parallel steps during a long day of exploring the city.

Plaza Sotomayor is at the center of town in Valpo. It's surrounded by an array of architectural styles, historic buildings, colorful, baroque, modern, and classical. There are open markets with fresh seafood and other goods. When I was there, the plaza also hosted an arts festival. Crowds in traditional Chilean garb roamed about, and there were dancers and performers and all manner of artists' booths. Plaza Sotomayor is a historic landmark in Chile. It was an exciting place to see.
I enjoyed wandering those lively streets atop the hill in Valparaiso. I stayed in a small inn and dined and floated leisurely through one weekend atop the hill.

The landscape in Valpo necessitates all manner of pathway and structure to climb the hillsides. On this passage, the stairs are painted the colors of the rainbow, all the way up. The walls around them are canvases for graffiti. The spot is a tourist landmark, the kind of place you take pictures of. I was not immune to its charm. I have some good pictures posing here.

As part of UNLV's International MFA program, I was required to travel abroad. We joked that it was our mandatory exile. There were no strict parameters for studying abroad. We received a sum from the department and applied for various other awards and whatever we got dictated what kind of trip we could afford. I ended up in Chile for three months over the summer. I went alone, staying in the heart of the city, in Bellas Artes, the arts district, in a rented one-bedroom apartment in a highrise overlooking the street. I took the subway all over town. I spoke no Spanish when I arrived. I didn't bring a cell phone. I didn't bring anything to read or do except be there in the present. It was probably the best experience I could have ever asked for. I went all over Santiago, that sophisticated jewel of a city. I forced myself to communicate as best I could and met local Chileans who were bilingual and kept me from feeling completely isolated. I wrote. I wrote a lot on that trip. I exercised, meditated. I used to spend the evenings on the balcony, listening to the street performers below. I will always miss Santiago, that place where the Andes frame the sky and the shops and cafes don't open until late morning. If I ever run away, it's where I'll go.

Bellas Artes is a bustling neighborhood in Santiago where I stayed for several months. I'd go to the bodega on the corner and buy snacks and cigarettes. The subway station was a great connector to the rest of the city. There were incredible musicians who performed on the corner below my apartment almost every night, singing Eduardo Gatti and Adele and other pop songs. It was a beautiful place. I didn't know anything about the neighborhoods in Santiago when I booked my stay. I just got lucky, trusting that the arts district would be my speed. And it was.

Palacio de La Moneda is the government headquarters where the president of Chile and other officials work. It's essentially the White House of Chile. It's a fine gray building with a large courtyard. I visited in the first week of my stay in Santiago with a tour guide in English and a group of international travelers. I passed the building several other times over the summer, too. It was where I learned more about Chile's history and the U.S. government's interference during Pinochet's coup. The scars on the building have been repaired, but they last in the stories told about those years in the 1970s when Chile suffered great harm. It's where president Allende was assassinated, where Pinochet operated his dictatorship. Today it remains the seat of the presidential branch of Chile's government and a major landmark. Of the culture in Santiago, it is affective–significant and complicated.

Location: Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos, Santiago, Chile
Description: This is probably the most formidable museum I have ever visited. The Museum of Memory and Human Rights directly addresses the atrocities of the Pinochet regime. There is a wall of photographs from the era, letters and testimonials from victims and their families, artifacts of abuse and torture. All of it is housed in an impressive structure. The exhibits sit with you for a long time after you leave. I'd suggest it for anyone visiting Chile.

Location: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombio, Santiago, Chile
Description: The Chilean Pre-Colombian Art Museum was a high point during my stay in Santiago. It has a remarkable collection of art from Mapuche, Incan, and other indigenous groups. I went more than once, discovered quipu, textiles, ceramics–some thousands of years old.

Location: Café de Las Artes, Santiago, Chile
Description: Some mornings, on slow days when I had slept in and didn't have much to do, I'd head down to this café and enjoy a brunch of coffee, cake, and cherimoya juice. It was a good little café with more sweets for breakfast than you could imagine.

In one of the most confusing and random events during my summer in Chile, I was invited to the gym by an acquaintance I made on the trip. Little did I know, it was an invitation to a boxing class. I was fighting for my life while a trainer screamed in Spanish, so loud and quick no words were coherent to me. My friend thought it was hilarious. She laughed and laughed while I sparred and jogged and so forth. Anyway, it was a good workout, but I didn't go back.
The Bellavista neighborhood in Santiago has a plaza with shops and restaurants. On more than one occasion, I spent an evening here, strolling the area and enjoying the food.

Guante is a shoe brand in Chile. I bought the best pair of urban boots here during my trip and wore them out walking all over the place. I wish I could get these shoes in the U.S. They're comfortable, well-crafted, and affordable.

Off the street of the pedestrian market in Santiago is this historic empanada restaurant. They were, without question, the best empanadas I have ever had. The place was always packed, with lines of people into the street. The empanadas were freshly baked, the smell pouring out of the kitchen where white clad bakers were busy churning them out. The decor was kitschy. There were no tables. You stood and ate your empanadas or took them with you. It made for a dizzying but fun experience.

This was a major landmark in the heart of Santiago. It's a castle on the hill, one with ponds, short cliffs, statues, gates. When I was there, it was open most days for pedestrians–a big, ascending park with marvelous views of the city. I walked around the castle a few times during that summer. It became the place from which I could orient myself, if I ever got lost.

Location: Virgen de la Inmaculada Concepcion, Santiago, Chile
Description: Above Santiago stands a statue of the Virgin Mary, some 40 feet tall. It's atop a mountain, too, way up above anything else. There's a park and a Catholic church and people make pilgrimages to pray under the statue. I went up once and it was quite the view. But most of the time, the statue atop the mountain helped me find my way in the city. It's visible from most places, a major landmark I could use to orient myself.

One evening, after a full day of adventures in the city, I enjoyed the best ceviche of my entire life on the rooftop of Casa Lastarria. It contained white fish, onions, potatoes, and leche de tigre (tiger's milk) which was cream and lemon juice. I think of it still to this day.

Location: Bauman Rare Books, Las Vegas, NV
Description: After I finished my MFA, I was incredibly fortunate to land a job at Bauman Rare Books as a rare bookseller. It's one of the premier rare book firms. Bauman has contributed to many of the finest collections. Their application process was competitive, intensive. Once hired, the training was extensive with months of handling inventory and studying book history. Training went on for the three years I worked there, too, because there was always more to learn. Eventually, I consulted major collectors and institutions. I handled some of the rarest books in the world. It was a defining experience for me. I'll forever be a bookseller now. But I'm glad to have moved on and started my own business (Evening Land Books). It allows me to enjoy the best parts of the book trade without the hassle of having a boss. But if you're ever in Las Vegas, I suggest visiting Bauman's gallery. It's in the Palazzo Casino on the Las Vegas Strip. It's a gem, a gallery of the finest things amidst the liveliness of the city. It's also where I met Kristina, my partner and dear love. Over long days in the gallery, we talked books and life and all manner of things, and fell in love. For all these reasons, I am grateful for my time at Bauman.

The classroom building on UNLV's campus is where I taught as an adjunct professor for three years after my MFA. I taught morning classes–first-year composition at 7AM. This was my own choice. I had a full-time, salaried position at Bauman Rare Books and needed to be there during the day, so teaching in the mornings was good for me. It also led to good batches of students, people who also had jobs to get to and full lives to live outside of college. Mature students. I developed course curriculum here as well. I was working in the computer classrooms and they afforded more tools for innovative writing instruction. Still, it was a lot of work on top of another job. Every semester, I would pause and consider whether to keep adjuncting, but I chose it every time. I learned in this building that I am an educator by nature. Adjuncting kept me in touch with academia, too, reaffirming my sense that I prefer to be in higher education.

There are many movie theaters in the Las Vegas valley, but I loved none was more  than Galaxy Theater. It didn't always show the best movies, but it had comfy recliners and good snacks. It was down the road from my apartment, too, and so I made a habit of going to the movies alone on a whim during the weekday evenings when I would have just crashed on my couch anyway. In those glorious months when MoviePass came out, I was there three times a week. I saw every garbage movie and every great one. It was a wonderful thing.

Hands down the best taco place I've ever been to. There's usually lines out the door. Tacos about three bucks apiece, served cafeteria style. Traditional Mexican tacos. Fresh cuts of carne asada, pollo, al pastor. The cooks in the back dicing and prepping in a flurry. I encourage you to go.

Location: Natural History Museum, Las Vegas, NV
Description: Once a month in 2017, I volunteered at the Las Vegas Natural History Museum, assisting in display setup and other tasks. I did it because I wanted the museum to flourish. It's small, under-served, but charming and well-managed. They have some notable donations from the casinos and they get occasional traveling exhibits from all over the country. It was a good experience. I got to construct replica battlements from the Roman Empire. I got to arrange taxidermy and fossils. I saw what it's like to manage a small museum. I hope that place continues to grow. The Las Vegas valley deserves more well-supported educational institutions.

Location: Route 91 Harvest Festival, Las Vegas, NV
Description: I was here, stuck in traffic, while a terrified crowd ran through the street and cars loaded with injured people and ambulances cut through the intersection after the worst mass shooting in American history. It was a traumatic event. I was safe in my car, but wholly confused and worried as the crowd stampeded away. It was true chaos along that part of the Las Vegas Strip. There were people running everywhere, and at the time, I had no idea what was going on. But it was obvious–palpable–from the crowd and the caravans of cars speeding away from the southern part of the Strip, and some truckbeds full of people holding on, following ambulances, that a tragedy had occurred. I still feel deeply about that shooting. I was already an advocate for gun reform in America. But nothing could have hardened my opinions more than that.

One morning on a week on Long Island, staying with a friend, we rose before the birds began chirping and drove along the Sunrise Highway, all the way to Montauk. There is a lighthouse there and a ledge that drops into the sea. We stood in the cold with the wind billowing against our coats and watched the sunrise over the Atlantic. It spread across the horizon, turning the water and the clouds purple, pink, and orange.

On one trip out East I stayed with a friend at his childhood home and enjoyed the ocean air, the small town sleepiness and the old brick buildings in Moriches. We went to dinky bars, drove around, returning in the evenings to this place. It was a joy to find villages so far from where I grew up but so familiar in that small town way.

Location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, NY
Description: If I ever lived in New York, I would probably visit the MET every week. When it's not busy, which is rare, it's a spectacular place to give the brain a spa treatment. The first time I went, I got lost for several hours in the galleries of the finest art, the contributions of geniuses from centuries and years ago around every corner. I walked wearing my headphones, listening to music and trying to pair the best songs with the best pieces in the museum. I love the Dutch Golden Age, Vermeer and Rembrandt, and the American Regionalists, Hopper and Benton, and the woodblock prints of Hokusai, and the magical realists of the Weimar Republic. It doesn't take a world-class museum to get the same sense of awe, but it doesn't hurt, either.

The movies and the myths got it right with Central Park. It's a magical place where on trips to New York, I've found myself wandering. I love that its flanked by the MET and the Natural History Museum and all manner of cultural spaces. New York would not be the best city without Central Park.

For the bibliophile, there is probably no better attraction in New York City than the Morgan Library. The murals, shelves, tall windows and marbled walls are a world-class display–but the books, the library room with the books is a haven for the mind.

After my first year at Bauman Rare Books, I had the pleasure of visiting the New York gallery, the flagship location, to meet my East Coast counterparts. I stayed for a week, working the floor in New York, going to dinner with the owners, exploring the hallways and bookshelves,  feeling royally treated by my employers. They have since moved locations, but for many decades this spot was Bauman's most prestigious gallery. It's a different universe in New York. The clients are the richest people in the world. There's an air of distinction to the book community, too. For much of the twentieth century, the city's Book Row was a central hub for the trade. It's a fraction of the size it once was, but businesses like Bauman Rare Books continue the legacy. They have since moved locations, but if you're ever in New York, I'd suggest stopping by the new gallery.

I went here several nights in a row for late dinners after full days on a work trip for Bauman Rare Books. It was down the way from my hotel. I enjoyed the snappy service, the true NY diner vibes. I ate alone and noticed many others, like me, middle class folks in Manhattan, probably visiting and working and looking for a relatively cheap meal.

In 2017, I stayed here on a trip paid for by my employer at the time, Bauman Rare Books. I spent long days in the gallery then went to dinner and drinks with my co-workers. It was a wonderful experience; although, I felt lots of expectation to express gratitude, first and foremost, as well as pressure to perform well for them in terms of selling expensive books. It very much was a "kiss the ring" trip. But after those peculiar days, I'd arrive back at the Park Central Hotel, relieved and exhausted. From my window, the bustling city below. New York from above. There is nowhere else to stay in that city except above it. And in turn, that trip and this hotel let me feel elevated. It was the first time an employer put me up in a nice place. I felt big then, despite the undertones of fealty. Those did not become so apparent until I reflected on the trip.

Location: Brooklyn Antiquarian Book Fair, Brooklyn, NY
Description: It may not have been the famous  ABAA-hosted International Antiquarian Book Fair, but the Brooklyn fair was still a treat. I went representing Bauman Rare Books. Over two days, I helped shop for rare editions and I worked the booth, all the while getting to know my co-workers from across the country. The Brooklyn fair is relatively small, but it brings in many of the world's best bookstores. Since New York is the antiquarian book capital of the world, any fair in the metro area is par excellence. That's not to say other book fairs in cities all over the U.S. aren't also great. I would suggest many of them. A good antiquarian book fair is like the Scholastic book fair but for adults.

It's as you would expect, a memorable cacaphony of screens and buildings and bright lights and people strewn about. A tourist trap. Iconic. But as far as tourist traps go, I prefer the Las Vegas Strip.

I went to the Association of Writers and Writing Programs conference (AWP) here in 2017 as an MFA student at UNLV. I worked the booth for the Black Mountain Institute and wandered the halls and attended panels and so forth. AWP is a major conference for creative writing programs, a special thing. The convention center in Washington DC is quite the complex. I enjoyed getting lost in the crowd.

I was in DC for the Association of Writers and Writing Programs conference. To escape the busyness and bustle of that socially taxing event, I went to the portrait gallery and got lost for hours. I'd put my headphones in, walk slowly and wait for something to move me. There are plenty of treasures in there.

Location: Smithsonian Museum of Natural History, Washington, DC
Description: I rank it second only to the American Museum of Natural History in New York; although, it is free admission here at the Smithsonian, so perhaps it ought to be number one. They have fossils, taxidermy, floors of many wonders. I'm pretty sure the ghost of Teddy Roosevelt comes out at night. Some day, I'd like to travel the world and visit all the best museums. It would take weeks in DC alone, days here. A boy can dream.

Location: Captain Daniel Packer Inne, Mystic, CT
Description: During a week staying on Long Island, my friends and I took a ferry across the Sound to Mystic, CT. We explored the historic seaside town on foot. Near the end of the long day, we meandered into Captain Daniel Packer Inne for supper. It was where I had the best clam chowder I've ever tasted. The place is old brick, old wood, colonial and quaint. There was an eery sense of dark history, of hard lives having been lived there. I think it was a time capsule of a place where the food and decor have hardly changed for centuries.

When I first moved to Las Vegas, there was a dirth of cultural institutions, especially museums. That city erected monuments of decadence and revelry then blew them up every decade. When the casinos went down, it was always a spectacle. Yet there were misty remembrances of those days gone by, the nostalgia for Old Las Vegas–cowboys, bandits, the Mob, Elvis. I think Las Vegas is still in the process of telling itself its own story, so when the Neon Museum opened, it was met with joy. It was needed. It captured something essential about the city and filled a void. It uses those remnants of old casinos and other structures and neon signs to tell the city's story. It is one of the most unique and enlightening museum experiences you'll ever have. It tops all the other attractions. It is something all cities should aspire to have.

Across the Colorado River at the southernmost tip of Nevada sits Bullhead City. There the water is clearer and colder than you'd ever imagine. It is quiet, the park near the river is friendly. I spent a weekend in Bullhead City on retreat. It was the spring of my graduation from UNLV and I needed the change of scenery. I breathed easy for that weekend, blessed and thankful for the river and the air and the break from those days of tribulation while I transitioned from graduate student to something else, then unknown.

Late in my time in Las Vegas, I discovered Is Sweet, a coffee and dessert spot open in the evenings. They have the best honey toast you'll ever find. They have crepe cakes, crème brulee, ice cream. If you're looking for a good place to go for dessert or late-night coffee, it is the best choice.

When I landed the job at Bauman Rare Books and I taught at UNLV as adjunct faculty, I became middle class. I made enough to buy a used Honda Accord and move into a nicer part of town. In this way, I felt that Mesa Ridge Apartments were an achievement for me. They weren't extravagant or anything, but it was more space to myself on the third floor of a modern apartment building. The pool was well maintained. I had a parking spot to myself. It was family owned and operated, they took pride in it, and so it was a pleasant place to be. But best of all was the mesa adjoining the apartment complex. It rose high above the buildings and you could climb to the top. From there, you could see a wide swath of the Las Vegas valley. It was also connected to a city park where pathways along the flat top of the mesa were carved out of the dirt. I loved living there as far as apartment living can go. The only issue was the freeway traffic. The freeway went right past the mesa and it echoed constantly.

I didn't know anyone else who frequented Skimos Coffee. This made it my favorite coffee shop for a while. It was down the street from my apartment where I lived during my Bauman and adjuncting years. At Skimos, the coffee was good and it was quiet and it was easy to focus.

There is a road to the beach in Sayulita that is decorated with streamers and banners of all colors. It's where you go for Instagram posts, to shop for knick-knacks, keepsakes, and momentos. It's the dream of a typical tourist in Mexico. Despite my snobbish proclivities, I was charmed.

It is exactly what you would imagine for an idyllic Mexican beach. When I was there, it was full of surfers, tan bodies, umbrellas, towels, perfect sand and greenblue tropical waters. It was packed with tourists. I didn't hate it, but I felt very out of place!

Not far down the sandy shore from the main beach in Sayulita was a secret beach, empty and secluded. We took the advice of a local and walked along the gravel road above the coastline, through a quiet, residential area with a couple restaurants that seemed to have been made from the remodeling of old houses. Then we talked down a rocky path to the sand. It was as clean and perfect as the primary beach in Sayulita, but we had it mostly to ourselves. Only the occasional stranger would walk by, or some beach dogs that were friendly and curious. I ran into the water, let the strong waves knock me down. I sat in the sand and felt revitalized. It was a beautiful place.

Location: Bahia de Banderas, Puerto Vallarta, JA
Description: Just south on the coast from Puerto Vallarta is the Bay of Flags, a range of cliffs and beaches and homes. I spent a week there during a friend's wedding in a massive coastal mansion. They rented it out. The whole wedding took place there. It was beautiful and quiet, save our raucous party. The Pacific spread itself wide across the sky. The weather was perfect. I can't deny that Mexico has some of the most beautiful coastline in the world.

Location: Intinarelli Home for Lost Children, Henderson, NV
Description: In this old neighborhood in Henderson (one of the oldest neighborhoods in the valley), my partner's family lives, the Intinarelli's. They are some of the kindest, most welcoming folks you will ever meet. Their house is informally known as the Intinarelli Home for Lost Children because they have made space for so many people over the years. This is not to say they're perfect or saintly. Nobody is. But if everyone built local communities as the Intinarellis do, the world would be a much better place.

The 2019 Association of Writers and Writing Programs (AWP) conference took place in Portland, OR. I went as a representative of Bauman Rare Books, technically, but really I was there to bask in the creative slendors of my fellow writers. Portland was great, too. I fell in love with that city. It has good food, walkable neighborhoods, a river running through it. Good, weird culture, too. It was one of my favorite AWP experiences. It was two years out from my MFA, but at that time my cohort was still in cahoots and we managed to catch up over the course of the week. I also connected with some book collectors. I felt like I was doing well professionally at that time. I wanted more out of my creative and professional work, but I felt like I was heading in the right direction during the week of the conference in Portland.

Location: Powell's City of Books, Portland, OR
Description: Among independent bookstores, Powell's in Portland stands out for its scale. There are multiple floors, sections, whole wings dedicated to subject areas. But it's also one of the greatest independent bookstores because of its service. It is clean, not dusty. It hires adequate amounts of staff. It does excellent work maintainnig a robust online presence. It's a jewel in Portland. When I was there for the AWP conference in 2019, I visited Powell's several times, just to breathe easy in my favorite kind of environment.

There may be no better way to get to know Portland than to attend it's Saturday Market. I perused its popups midday as a respite from the conference. There is a whole blessed community of sellers, tinkerers, textilists, foodies, artists. It is one of the best popup markets I've ever found.

One thing you may not know about Portland is that it has excellent American classics at a ton of local restaurants. It was here at the Tabor Tavern, for example, that I had the best macaroni & cheese of my entire life. It's a foodie town. Highly recommend.

There's so much I could write about Downtown Las Vegas––most of it lovely––but my starkest memory of this place is probably the George Floyd protests in 2020. It was the first time I'd left my apartment in weeks. The pandemic was already putting us on edge. But then, that footage came out and there were scenes from every major city in America. I felt I had to take a stand, and so I went downtown where there were protests planned. Unfortunately, things did not stay peaceful. There were some unruly elements to the crowd, but I don't think it would have been so messy had the police not shown so much force. There were walls of them confronting the protesters, and SWAT vehicles driving around. I saw at least SWAT truck arbitrarily launching tear gas canisters at groups on the street. The police marched at folks, barricaded their routes. They were more pushy than the protesters. It's a shame that's the memory that comes up when I think of downtown. The truth is that far more good memories sprout from here––dates I had, nights out with friends. But downtown Las Vegas has a little of everything, and so not all of it is good.

Here just past the border with Nevada is a speed trap. The Idaho state police are a repugnant lot. They have nothing better to do than wait for hours at the border to slap a big fine on someone. Once, that someone was me. That's how I know. But I was only going a few miles over! It didn't matter. Not to Officer Filbert who was maybe 24 years old and eager to flex his badge-given powers. Anyway, you've been warned. The speed trap is right at these coordinates.

There are a few ways to reveal the Palouse in its most essential form. You can drive through its highways and county roads and catch glimpses of that green, yellow, and blue from the tops of its foreboding hills. You can see it from the air, looking out by plane, where the unreal, shadeless hillsides spread out as America the Beautiful, spacious skies, perfect amber waves of grain. But probably the best way to take in this peculiar landscape is to climb the Kamiak Butte. The hike is not long. It cuts through pines and crags until its peak opens the view–nothing but sky and wheat for miles. It was just the first couple weeks in Pullman when I made the ascent for the first time. In my two years in Pullman, no other spot assured me of the virtues of that place more than the peak of Kamiak Butte.

Ferdinand's is the official creamery of Washington State University. Does a campus need an official creamery? After enjoying Ferdinand's for two years, I'd say, yes, absolutely. Folks rave about the ice cream, which is good, but I'm a bit of an ice cream snob after growing up in Minnesota where people take it seriously. But I've got to hand it to Ferdinand's cheeses, especially the World Famous Cougar Gold Cheddar. That's some good stuff. People drive across the state to buy it. Sorry, Wisconsin, but I have to say it: it's the best American cheddar I've ever enjoyed.

In 2020, at the onset of the COVID-19  pandemic, I quit my jobs in Las Vegas and moved to Pullman, WA, to continue my graduate studies. Washington State University could not have been a better place for that period in my life. I completed an MA in Literary Studies and a Graduate Certificate in Digital Humanities there. The English Department was exceptional. They helped me commit myself to the digital humanities and gain new skills and experiences. It's a good community in the English Department. I miss those folks often.

Look, I know you probably don't think of Pullman as a mecca of exceptional dining experiences, but there's one place there that ranks among the best anywhere, at least for brunch. The Old European serves German potato pancakes, Swedish hot cakes, and Aebelskivers. They have freshly squeezed orange juice. The decor matches the Anglo-European menu with  spindle chairs, dimly lit chandeliers, and wooden plaques written in Gothic fonts. It's good, it's worth a try. It's not like you're transported to the olden times or anything, but the food is delicious and the ambiance matches the menu.

We all had our places during the pandemic, those spots we were stuck in, or the spots we felt were safe. I came to know McGee park so well those months, years. Four times a day, I'd walk along its concrete path or cut through the grass with the dogs. The park had a little playground, an island of trees, a small baseball diamond, a fenceline buried in the brush. There was nothing special about it, but if you walk through a place that often, the details are enriched and the smallest of happenings become vivid memories. I remember seeing a fox there on a crisp Autumn morning. I remember catching sight of a family of racoons up in a tree. I remember one winter morning after a snowfall when a snowman stood in the center of the field, left by some artist in the night. I remember other dogwalkers and the distance we kept for the sake of our pets and our own health. McGee Park–of all the places in Pullman, none crystalize my memory so well.

Pullman is a town built upon the steepest hillsides that qualify as hills before you might elevate them to the status of buttes or plateaus. It's like if there were foothills without mountains. You know those steep ascents that are technically walkable but knock the wind out of you, right before the crags shoot up and make it a mountain? That's what Pullman is like in every direction. Anyway, throughout my MA at Washington State University–and throughout the pandemic–I lived atop College Hill. It was mostly quiet save the occasional house party. It was dreadful to drive up after a winter snow. The highlight of my life there was the day a moose wandered into town and trotted up College Hill. It made the news. It's a magical place. Aside from the unfortunate frat drinking culture, College Hill is quite lovely.

It was here at this little corner of the Washington State University campus that I first returned to in-person events during the pandemic. I taught undergraduate classes here. I was the assistant director of the computer lab. Throughout my time at WSU, I never had an in-person graduate class, but in my teaching and administrative roles, I was expected to show up in the flesh. Unfortunately, the pandemic colors my memories at Avery Hall, but I'll say the community in the English Department there was the best of any community I've met at a large university. From the students to the staff to the faculty, the people there deserve every good thing afforded to them. It is a building of kindness.

The fanciest restaurant in Pullman. We went here whenever family visited, whenever there were celebrations to be had. They make an exceptional roasted chicken. The interior is dimly lit, wood grain, sort of lounge-like but with some rustic kitchen vibes as well. It feels like any nice restaurant inside, but you can't escape the Pullman wilderness, not even at the Black Cypress. One time, while my cousin visited, we sat near the windows and in the middle of our dinner,  a fox ran right past the restaurant, just jaunting down the sidewalk through the middle of town. That's Pullman for you. And the Black Cypress is part of it.

Pups & Cups was charming proof of the dog-friendly culture in town. Lots of good dogs sat calmly at the feet of their humans. Some bad dogs were there too, restless pups, but that was always okay with me. The establishment had a gated back room where you could let your eager pooches run around and play, if that's what they needed. Could there be a better business model? Good coffee and happy dogs?

In 2020, I sold my car and bought myself a bike. It was a health conscious and environmentally conscious decision that I will forever be grateful I made. I suppose that's its own story, but this place in the form of a business helped me transition to becoming a bike commuter. B & L Bicycles is an excellent shop. They have all the info, services, and merchandise to get you on the road or trail. I didn't just buy from them, I learned from them. They taught me how to accomodate myself without a car. That's the potential of small businesses. I wish we supported the good ones more often.

One day early in my time in Pullman, I biked around the way, exploring. It was a crisp Autumn day and the hills looked lovely. I made it up a steep hill then coasted down the other side until a tall fence came into view, and behind the fence, what looked like a rustic jungle gym. It had tractor tires, wood beams, mounds of dirt. As I came closer, I suddenly noticed a large brown hump appear behind one of the mounds. I got closer still, stopped, and squinted to see. It was a grizzly bear adjusting itself as it bathed in the sun. Then more movement, and I made out another bear. Then another. There were several lazing about. They paid me no mind. The fenceline led to a parking area and a building, the WSU Bear Center. Why was it there? I have no idea, but I'm grateful for it. Who doesn't love discovering an enclosure full of bears?

Location: Hungry Hippie Tacos, Grand Marais, MN
Description: You'll notice most of the locations in Grand Marais harken back to my childhood, but not Hungry Hippie Tacos. I discovered this place on a weekend getaway with my beloved. Now, I don't think anyone will believe me. I know it sounds crazy. But the fact is, Hungry Hippie Tacos is the best taco joint on the planet. They have fry bread tortillas, smoked meats, fresh ingredients. They don't try to be traditional Mexican tacos. That would be absurd. Instead, they're like this perfect blend of the best taco meats, Midwest comfort foods, a hint of BBQ traditions, and the freshness of some California yuppy lunch spot. You've just got to try it. The place also captures something fundamental about Grand Marais culture. It's whimsical, inclusive, crunchy but not stuffy. It's the best Minnesota has to offer.

Hudson's hamburgers rank high among those I've eaten. They've been in business for over a century. They are a staple in the community of Coeur d'Alene. No frills, just quality flat-top burgers and fresh buns. In a town so desperate to seem quintessentially American, Hudson's makes the strongest case. But that being said, I prefer Smith Burger Co. in Champaign, IL, or the Lion's Tap in Eden Prairie, MN. Both have better service, too. Hudson's always has long lines out the door. But still, that's about number three on my list of Greatest Burger Joints of All Time, so it's worth a stop.

Riverfront Park is the built enviroment along the edge of the Spokane River where it splits in three and cascades down the falls. The park is in the center of town. It's the most beautiful part of Spokane. You can meander through it in an hour, it's not large. There is not much to Spokane, so thank God they bothered to build the Riverfront Park.

Location: Giant White Pine Trailhead, Harvard, ID
Description: A friend of mine came out to visit in 2021. We decided to explore the mountains and the hills to the East. We drove a while from Pullman, picking random trails off Google Maps. Out there, you can find trails into the forests with ease. We eventually settled on the Giant White Pine Trailhead and made our way. The giant White Pine marking the start of the trail was felled sometime ago, but it still lays there. The trail goes through switches and cuts in the forest, through clearings left by the lumber industry, up the ridges of steep hills. Up and up we went, catching up and letting the dogs run ahead. We didn't find anything in particular. The trail went further than you could walk in a day. Hiking is funny that way. You just pick a trail and go and you're lucky if it leads anywhere. It usually doesn't.

Out there in the hilly Palouse is a waterfall and gorge that proves to be the most exquisite landmark imaginable. You'd never be able to spot it from afar. You have to drive down some empty county roads until you reach a parking area. Then you have to get out of the car and walk to what looks like just another drop in the hills. But then, you'll see it, the rocky crags and the water falling dramatically into a wide pool. It probably drops 100 feet or more. The surrounding area is desert, plain and brown, but in this one space between hillsides, it's a majestic waterway, a landmark. You'll never find a better spot.

This trailhead sits at the edge of town. It leads to Moscow, ID. I used to bike the trail to get some exercise. It's  non-descript, just a paved trail running parallel to the highway, but I'll remember it forever as that place I could clear my head.

It sounds like an enchanted mythological place, the Magpie Forest. But in reality, it's a quaint brushy hilltop with narrow trails. I found it by happenstance one day while walking the dogs. It provides nice views of the valleys below and it gives you the sense that you're living in an Andrew Wyeth painting. There are some images in my mind from the Magpie Forest that make up the collage of my idea of Pullman. It is an essential place.

Location: Pullman Village Centre Cinemas, Pullman, WA
Description: During the pandemic, I missed going to the movies. It's always been one of my favorite pastimes. So when the local Pullman theater reopened, I was elated, excited–so much so that I even began emailing the manager, requesting new films. There's a universality to local movie theaters. They are all the same place. The popcorn, candy, lobbies with posters and funny patterns in the carpet. When the theater reopened, I inquired about the Green Knight starring Dev Patel. They brought it in. That's another fun fact about local movie theaters. Sometimes, they'll take requests! What a joy it was to go back to that familiar place after being cooped up for so long, to be welcomed with a new film depicting an ancient story.

It's a classic diner experience. The building looks like an Airstream trailer–ovular with aluminum sides. The booths are cushioned with that bouncy faux-leather. The food is quick, cheap, and filling. The coffee isn't too bad. I love a good diner. The Moscow Diner was always exactly what I needed it to be.

The downtown stretch of Moscow, ID, was a pleasant experience on the weekends in the spring and fall during my time at Washington State University. Once things began reopening during the pandemic, we'd putz carefully outdoors at the farmer's market or check out the quiet antique shops. Moscow presents dueling cultures of progressive inclusiveness and artistry on the one hand versus Christian nationalist oppression on the other. We went downtown to support those forward-thinking businesses in particular. Idaho needs them badly. It needs culturally progressive loci like downtown Moscow. It's a safe harbor for many folks who live in an otherwise oppressive and unwelcoming state.

If you're looking for a deep, meandering used bookstore, there are few more appropriate than Myopic Books. It's a longstanding establishment in the Wicker Park neighborhood of Chicago. I wouldn't expect to find rare books here, but you'll be pleased with the bohemian atmosphere and artistic fervor and good reading copies. I stop by whenever I'm in Chicago for the atmosphere alone.

Auntie's Bookstore is probably my favorite business in Spokane. It's a superb independent bookstore, the kind of place that sells mostly new books, but some used books as well. It's like Barnes & Noble but with all the corporate homogeneity stripped away. The interior is welcoming. There are two floors and separate rooms to get lost in. I'd stop by every once in a while and buy a book I didn't need, just to support them. One time, I was approached by a woman carrying a recorder, notepad, and pencil. She asked me what book I'd like to see turned into a movie. My answer was One Hundred Years of Solitude. It turns out, she was a reporter doing a fluff piece for the local paper, The Inlander. My answer made the news.

In 2022, I arrived at the University of Illinois to complete a PhD in Information Science. I remember my first impressions of the campus and the town. It was everything you'd expect of an elite university–expansive courtyards, incredible architecture, the invigorating air of intellectual pursuits and youthful promise. I don't think there could be a more perfect example of an American college  in terms of UIUC's embodiments of that larger category of place. I'm thankful for it. As far as built environments go, there are few–if any–more hospitable than American universities.

The School of Information Sciences–the iSchool for short–is my disciplinary home now. I wish I had known about the information sciences from the start of my academic career; although, I don't think I'd change the other degrees I've earned en route to this field. I would have just aimed for it at the onset. It's a perfect blend of library sciences,  humanities, computer science, and data science. It's where those fields overlap on Venn diagrams. In my particular subset, it's where I can pursue research in natural language processing, AI, digital humanities, computer programming, US literary history, creative writing, place studies, and cultural analytics. The iSchool has armed me with technical skills and taught me how to meld computational methods with humanities research.

On special dates, Kristina and I enjoy sushi, and this is the best sushi restaurant in town. In fact, I've never been here without Kristina. It's been our unspoken spot for noteworthy date nights, just the two of us.

For decades, the Midwest Antiquarian Booksellers Association has hosted the Chicago Book & Paper Fair here at the Union Hall. It's an extravaganza of books–rare, used, antiquarian, ephemera, etc. I've gone as an exhibitor with Evening Land Books and as a customer. In either case, it's delightful. Why don't more people attend these things? They are the bibliophile's dream!

There is no better burger in Chicago than Au Cheval's butter burger with bacon. But you must go to the original location. You must suffer through lighting far too dim, through music way too loud. It's always busy, too. But by God, that burger is delicious. I'd also suggest the hashbrowns with duck gravy. You will never forget it.

The museum is tucked between highrise apartments and sprawling courtyards. The walls, white stucco. The roof, clay. It's one of those buildings that doesn't look too large from the outside, but once inside you realize the scale of the place. It's one of the best Native American art museums in the world. There are textiles, ornaments, jewelry, statues, murals, displays. They reminded me how much I didn't know. I went with my in-laws and so part of my visit was concerned with pleasing the group. But if I could have stayed longer, I would have lingered around the kachina dolls. They were startling, their elaborate features communicated some reverent power I could not comprehend.

Let me just preface that in my childhood, my idea of tacos were those out-of-the-box hardshells filled with pan-fried ground beef mixed with a packet of taco seasoning. We used to have them for dinner, the Midwest taco. I always skipped the sour cream, but boy was it available on taco nights in my family. Anyway, that's the preface for me saying that Maize Mexican Grill makes good tacos. They are the best in Chambana. They aren't as good as the authentic tacos I came to enjoy in Las Vegas, but they're definitely not the usual Midwest variety.

Cheeseburgers have always been my comfort food. I'll eat just about any cheeseburger on the planet, but it was with great fortune that I discovered Smith Burger Company early in my time in Champaign. They are quality burgers–affordable, delicious. After a good workout or a long day, Kristina and I often fall back to Smith Burger Company.

At the time of this writing, I live in this general vicinity and I operate a small business–Evening Land Books–out of my home. It's a rare and collectible bookstore. It's entirely for fun, but it also helps to pay the bills! If I could give you any advice in life, it's that you should try to monetize your hobbies. For me, that meant turning my book collecting pastime into a little online shop.

At the start of 2024, I attended Kristina's family reunion here in Scottsdale. It was my first time in the Phoenix area. We stayed in an AirBnB with the whole family. It was desert surburbia. Sunny, warm. I'll be honest, my sense of the place was that it was homogenous. I think Scottsdale has a lot of potential, but it reeked of retired Baby Boomers who prefer Olive Garden over local restaurants, who want to drive everywhere and never walk. That's just not my vibe. The one exception was maybe Old Town where pedestrian-friendly streets are lined with small businesses. But even there, a lot of it seemed insincere, like it was staged for tourists.
On a sunny September day, I proposed to the love of my life here at the top of Art Hill, overlooking the waterways and grassy fields and forests. She said yes!

Location: Missouri History Museum, St. Louis, MO
Description: I went here with Kristina during a long weekend in town. It is a superb museum with exhibits on Missouri history, broadly construed. There's everything from westward expansion to local LGBTQ history to the St. Louis World's Fair. I came to love it. If you want to understand the zeitgeists of St. Louis (and U.S.) history, it is a great spot to visit.

Location: St. Louis Art Museum, St. Louis, MO
Description: In the midst of a twitterpated fog, Kristina and I attempted to enjoy the St. Louis Art Museum right after I proposed. We walked around, giddy like children, completely unable to appreciate art or anything else. It was a great moment, quite honestly, but I couldn't actually tell you anything about this museum–other than it was free, welcoming, spacious, a good place to stroll with your love, whether you plan to appreciate the art or not.

Location: Mississippi River Overlook, St. Louis, MO
Description: Across the river from St. Louis, there's this large park with a long ramp leading up to an overlook. It gives you a remarkable view of the city skyline, one centered on that unique landmark, the arch. It's the oddest thing–this overlook is not easy to find. It's nestled between some freeway ramps, train tracks, a dumpy-looking casino, and a grain loader. But I'm certain it's the best view of St. Louis, or at least the Gateway Arch.

Kristina and I went to Carmine's in those giddy hours after I proposed. For that reason, my memory of the restaurant is embued with a kind of disbelief. The browns and reds were richer, warmer. The mural on the back wall was incomprehensible, either because of my emotional state or because it objectively was (I'm not sure which). The food was great–steaks, deep-fried ravioli, frog legs. The place is a landmark in St. Louis, that much I know for certain. I would recommend it for tourists wanting a relatively affordable steak dinner under the imposing shadow of the Gateway Arch.

Location: Taste of Black St. Louis, St. Louis, MO
Description: In the park right next to the Soldiers Memorial, there was a crowd and music and vendors in tents and food trucks. There were banners of red, black, yellow, and green. Lines wrapped around the most popular vendors. Families, couples on dates, teenagers in gaggles, enjoying some unsupervised fun. We walked around, Kristina and I, and we ate a ton of food–fried plantains, ox tails, pinneapples hollowed out and filled with candy. All the vendors were small businesses serving up an incredible range of food. It's a great little event in St. Louis. We were lucky to be there in 2024.

The debates surrounding regional pizza variations are emblematic of the unifying national culture of the United States. Different cities, regions, and states in the larger U.S. lay claim to the defining aspects of its national culture. Through pizza, they have an innocuous aspect–something that can be debated and tested and ranked, but ultimately, it's of little consequence. It's a safe way to push and pull over larger national cultural norms and tropes. The result is wonderfully diverse pizzas, too, and St. Louis-style pizza is a great example. While it's not often as celebrated as something like New York-style pizza, I'd put it near the top of the list of great pizza variations. It's got a thin crust with tomato sauce and provel cheese. It's good, very good. The cheese really makes it distinct from other regional pizzas. It's this really gooey, buttery, almost smokey cheese. It goes well with sausage, pepper, and mushroom toppings. Imo's Pizza is the longstanding regional chain. Locals may find Imo's a tired example of their signature pizza, but for any tourists, I'd highly recommend it.

I think the Gateway Arch is the most distinct architectual landmark in America. Its scale and glimmering edges reach above most of St. Louis. Somehow, it stands without teetering or swaying. It's otherworldly, an extraterrestrial chain link planted firmly into the earth, ready for a hook to clasp it and pull us out of orbit.

Of all the Midwest cities, none is so fogged in its own nostalgia than St. Louis. Its inhabitants walk around in the shadow of the early twentieth century, still concerned with things like the World's Fair and Charles Lindbergh and Miles Davis and Maya Angelou. They are certain Louis Sullivan will complete another skyscraper soon. There's an air of industry, expansion, bright futures. Yet in the presence unseen in the culture of the city, nothing changes. The same families of means stay rich in their impeccable houses, the same streets are maintained even after so many cars have driven away. No one notices the central heart of America anymore, except its clouded nostalgic self. It's a time capsule of a place, if you shut your eyes and imagine what it must have been like, what it always was and is.

Across the river a ways from St. Louis, down some unassuming roads, are the remnants of America's largest pre-Colombian city, Cahokia. You can walk around the complex, read the signs at kiosks that describe the greatest landmark in America. You can climb atop its largest extant mounds, grassy and steep. The absence of buildings gives the area a sense of possibility. It is purely topographic. But this quality elides the true nature of the place. It is a built environment, platformed, arranged, celestial. When you visit Cahokia, you are transported to a different cultural and historical plane, one not typically assembled in our Western colonial tradition. It is the true history of the region. How do I know this? You need only go there and imagine its former structures and people covering the place, preceding everything else that you know about America.

Location: Valley Crossing Elementary School, Woodbury, MN
Description: Here begins my formal education. I arrived here for Kindergarten, but much to my parent's surprise, the school said I was too old for Kindergarten. I had missed it by a year. So, instead my younger sister went to Kindergarten and I immediately went to first grade. My mother was the one who always dropped us off on her way to work. It was a big school with flat fields, playgrounds, and lots of kids in open wings where the classrooms were divided by retractable walls that looked like giant cloth accordions. I remember always sitting on the floor. And I remember being timed for the mile, and being impressed with how fast the older kids could run it. During recess, my friends and I formed the Shark Club. It was a brief period in which I was obsessed with sharks, after having watched Jaws. But then, my mother got a new job and this school was no longer on her route to work, so my sister and I were enrolled elsewhere.
